ASRSN:2164164.n: On a flight as the instructor for a student we entered steep turns and during the turn the door open warning light came on. I looked back and saw the rear door had come un-latched and was only hanging on by a retention clasp and was bouncing around. I didn't want to lose the door so I grabbed the handle and asked the student to end the maneuver and level off, and when he did the door blew open and broke free of the aircraft. I then took the controls from the student and re-entered the pattern at ZZZ and landed the aircraft. I was rattled and just wanted to get the plane on the ground. The door was closed and checked before take off so I don't know how or why it came open, and I did not get a chance to follow the door open checklist.
ASRSN:2164164.s: During steep turns in a training flight, the instructor observed the rear door unlatch and bounce before it blew off the aircraft upon leveling. The instructor landed safely at ZZZ, noting the door was secured before takeoff and the cause remained unknown.

ASRSN:2164168.n: After departing ZZZ for ZZZ1, about 15 minutes into flight, Aircraft's electrical system started pulling amps from battery. STBY Power was not producing any output. Center was contacted, and a return to ZZZ was initiated. No assistance was requested, nor was any priority handling requested. Gradually, electrical system was pulling more and more from Battery with -11AMPS being drawn at the time of landing. Aircraft landed safely in ZZZ, and was subsequently written up in aircraft logbook. This is the third write-up for the same issue in this aircraft. PA was made to Passenger in flight, as well as on the ground. Passenger was rebooked on the next ZZZ1 flight.
ASRSN:2164168.s: The flight crew returned to ZZZ after the aircraft's electrical system began drawing excessive battery current and standby power failed. The aircraft landed safely with -11 amps drawn, marking the third logbook entry for this recurring issue, while passengers were rebooked on the next flight.

ASRSN:2164177.n: While conducting Phase 1 Flight Testing In Accordance With (IAW) Advisory Circulars 90-116 and 90-89C at the airplane's home base (ZZZ), the right main landing gear of Aircraft X partially collapsed during a long / straight roll out, following a LLWS encounter and Crosswind landing. Upon a normal touchdown, the LLWS raised the right wing...an immediate correction was made a the airplane continued its normal rollout on all three (3) wheels.The right wingtip and fully extended (45 degrees) right flap slowly contacted the Runway surface, as the airspeed decreased. The airplane came to rest on the Runway in the longitudinal direction of travel and parallel to the Runway Centerline.The airplane was manually righted and the place on its landing gear (tricycle configuration). It was pushed back to its hangar.The Airport Manager subsequently reopened this Class G Airport.There were no injuries to either Pilot.
ASRSN:2164177.s: During Phase 1 flight testing at ZZZ, Aircraft X's right main landing gear partially collapsed after a low-level wind shear encounter and crosswind landing caused the right wingtip and flap to contact the runway. The aircraft was manually righted and towed to the hangar with no pilot injuries.

ASRSN:2164217.n: Upon taxi into gate the Captain had begun his turn to commit to the gate with idle thrust due to the jet blast hazard of the tightly spaced gates. After the turn was completed a baggage cart with bags under tow drove through the safe area. It was determined by the crew as well as the marshaller that safe distance could not be maintained so the aircraft came to a stop and the parking brake was set. Due to the close proximity of gates and jet blast hazard the aircraft had to be towed to the gate. A call was made to operations notifying them of the tow in, a PA was made to the passengers regarding the tow in, and supplemental procedures for aircraft tow in were applied. While turning into gate we noticed a ramp tug with baggage carts attached turn towards us at our 10 o'clock position. The tug driver stopped as we were approaching the start of the lead-in line and it looked too close to proceed. The marshaller also noticed the incursion and gave us the stop signal with his wands. We shutdown both engines and notified operations that we would need to be towed into the gate now, as we could no longer apply engine thrust due to jet blast concerns after committing to the turn. We informed the flight attendants and the passengers over the PA that we were now a tow in.
ASRSN:2164217.s: The flight crew aborted a taxi-in due to a baggage cart incursion at the gate, where jet blast hazards prevented maintaining safe distance. Consequently, the aircraft was shut down and required a tow to the gate after the marshaller signaled a stop.

ASRSN:2164230.n: Uncommanded Roll with Auto Pilot Engaged with associate ROLL AUTHORITY voice alert and amber indication on Primary Flight Display (PFD). We were 7 mile final and 2000'. Auto pilot engaged. No other aircraft on final. Arrival had pockets of turbulence but approach was mostly smooth. The uncommanded roll was induced by the aircraft. PF immediately disconnected A/P and the rest of the approach was uneventful. I submitted Electronic Log Book (ELB) report and met MX at aircraft to debrief. Established on final for runway XXR with the autopilot on and fully configured roughly 7 miles out from the runway the roll authority amber light on the PFD populated and the plane isolated slightly to the left, we were not following another aircraft up close. I immediately disconnected the autopilot and continue the approach without further incidence. The Amber indication in the PFD extinguished. Conditions were normal for a semi windy approach into ZZZ.
ASRSN:2164230.s: The flight crew experienced an uncommanded left roll with a ROLL AUTHORITY alert on the PFD while 7 miles final at 2,000 feet with autopilot engaged. The pilot immediately disconnected the autopilot, the indication extinguished, and the approach was completed without further incident.

ASRSN:2164232.n: Due to there not being enough dry ice securing our Dangerous Goods (DG), we were made to return to gate.
ASRSN:2164232.s: The crew returned to the gate because insufficient dry ice was used to secure the Dangerous Goods.

ASRSN:2164238.n: Conducting an Autoland in visual conditions to clear MEL limiting approaches to Land 2. Briefed autoland advised tower conducting autoland tower reported sensitive area would not be protected. At 75' aircraft began an uncommanded roll to the right. Disconnected autopilot corrected and landed. Reported unsuccessful autoland in ACARS and as a precaution entered and maintenance write up.
ASRSN:2164238.s: The pilot conducting an autoland to Land 2 reported an uncommanded right roll at 75 feet after the tower stated the sensitive area would not be protected. The pilot disconnected the autopilot, corrected the aircraft, and landed safely, subsequently logging a maintenance write-up.

ASRSN:2164265.n: Immediately on departure off Runway 30R at BJC we experienced a total loss of GPS reception along with associated systems. We were busy flying so didn't have time to note everything that was affected but it was the typical stuff associated with loss of GPS, such as TAWS, synthetic vision, etc. The HSI (Horizontal Situation Indicator) seemed to continue to function fine and we were able to fly the assigned heading after takeoff. It did make a high workload departure even more demanding as we had that distraction plus a TCAS TA - not RA - plus Tower advising us of traffic and a turn all simultaneously. After about 60 - 90 seconds the GPS returned to working as normal. I suspected a GPS jammer was located near the end of the runway. We reported the GPS anomaly to ATC a minute or two later and another aircraft reported similar problems in the exact same area we had it. I also emailed the Chief Pilot to report it in case other Company aircraft were arriving or departing BJC or flying in the Denver area that day. We experienced no other GPS issues that flight or the rest of the day. We have had the aircraft for several days prior to this even with no GPS issues during that time either. No suggestions. I don't believe there were any malfunctions in the aircraft. I believe this was an external event likely caused by a local jammer or some other local anomaly that interfered with the GPS signal.
ASRSN:2164265.s: The crew experienced a temporary total GPS loss with associated system failures immediately after departing Runway 30R at BJC, increasing workload during a TCAS TA and traffic advisory. The reporter suspects an external jammer near the runway caused the anomaly, as another aircraft reported similar issues in the same area before signals returned to normal.

ASRSN:2164315.n: On approach to runway XXR in ZZZ aircraft was stabilized well prior to 1000 ft at about 100' the aircraft was about 5 knots slow and I alerted the PF that we were slow, the PF added power, the airplane touched down, and bounced up into the air, the spoilers had not deployed as confirmed by the ecam, the PF began to derotate and it felt like the main wheels were not on the ground and the spoilers still had not deployed, i stated we are still airborne, we bounced". A go around was called and carried out, during the go around the tail touched the runway as observed by maintenance. We didn't feel the tail touch the runway. I don't feel it was a hard initial touchdown, but with the thrust not at idle the spoilers didn't deploy which caused the plane to skip off the ground.Thrust not being at idle at touchdown caused the spoilers not to deploy and airplane to skip off the runway. Advancing thrust and retracting flaps diverted my attention from monitoring the pitch attitude on rotation off the runway."
ASRSN:2164315.s: The PM and PF in a ZZZ aircraft experienced a bounced landing on approach to runway XXR because thrust was not at idle, preventing spoiler deployment. A subsequent go-around resulted in a tail strike observed by maintenance, attributed to the crew's distraction while managing thrust and flaps.

ASRSN:2164426.n: I was the PIC and CFI-G in the glider. The towplane was getting close to our release altitude when I noticed another aircraft approaching slightly higher and converging. The pitch angle of the towplane had prevented the pilot from seeing the oncoming traffic until we had closed within the mentioned distance. At that time he executed at left turn. At no time did I see any indication from the other plane that they ever saw us approaching.
ASRSN:2164426.s: The PIC/CFI-G in a glider reported a near mid-air collision during tow when the towplane's pitch angle blocked the pilot's view of converging traffic. The towplane pilot executed a left turn to avoid the other aircraft, which showed no indication of seeing them.

ASRSN:2164428.n: While completing touch and go's on RWY 36 at 7F3, a plane announced his intention to depart from runway 13, at the time we were in a left downwind for 36 and traffic departing 13 would not be a factor. Once the plane departed from 13 he subsequently made a left hand traffic pattern, after touching down on runway 36 I started my departure climb and the plane announced he was on the base leg for runway 13, my flight instructor occupying the right seat made visual contact of the plane was who was at our 1' o'clock roughly 200 feet vertically and horizontally from us. Had we not started our crosswind turn early and aggressively we would have potentially lost separation with the plane.
ASRSN:2164428.s: A pilot and instructor conducting touch-and-goes at 7F3 encountered a departing aircraft on a left traffic pattern for Runway 13 while climbing from Runway 36. The other aircraft appeared at 1 o'clock, 200 feet away, requiring an aggressive early crosswind turn to maintain separation.

ASRSN:2164457.n: Took off from ZZZ1 with no issues, while heading to ZZZ for pattern work. On our first touch and go, we lost approximately 400 RPM about 200ft above the runway on takeoff. I pitched down and began to run engine failure checklist, but before I began the RPMs came back. We lost power for about a total of 10 seconds which caused us to lose altitude. I circled above the airport to regain altitude before returning back to ZZZ1 safely. The reason for the report is this is not the first time this situation has occurred. I am an experienced instructor and former student of the program and it concerns me that this has happened approximately 6-10 times in the last two weeks. Additionally, I have also been very involved in maintenance recovery flights for about a year and we have never had this issue till about 2-3 months ago.
ASRSN:2164457.s: An instructor pilot reported a 400 RPM loss at 200 feet during a touch-and-go takeoff at ZZZ1, causing a 10-second power loss and altitude decrease before recovery. The pilot noted this recurring issue has occurred 6–10 times in two weeks, raising concerns about recent engine reliability.

ASRSN:2164458.n: Engine was approaching Oil Temp red-line as I approached the VFR East Transition. Attempts to cool the engine (Mixture, Airspeed) were unhelpful as it continued to trend towards overheating. Informed Local TRACON about my diversion back to my home-airport. I cannot recall what altitude instructions if any were provided as I cut through the Bravo airspace, Possibly cut into ZZZ Delta before making Contact and being cleared in.
ASRSN:2164458.s: The pilot reported an engine oil temperature approaching the red-line while approaching the VFR East Transition. Despite cooling attempts, the pilot diverted home, cutting through Bravo airspace and possibly ZZZ Delta before receiving clearance.

ASRSN:2164481.n: I was the pilot not flying (PNF) flying Aircraft X a Dash 8-400. We departed ZZZ from Runway XX with two crew members (no passengers) on board for a ferry flight bound for ZZZ1. The aircraft was operating on a FAA Ferry Flight Permit, as it had been in storage at ZZZ for several months. During this time, a third party was contracted to maintain the required maintenance schedule for the aircraft. Prior to our departure contract maintenance had just completed a power assurance check and all was deemed OK for the ferry flight.After departure we contacted ZZZ Departure and we flew the obstacle departure procedure for Runway XX. Departure gave us a vector and climb. While in the right turn and climbing through 7-8,000' onto the new heading, we experienced a No.1 BLEED HOT Warning. The bleed air switch for the NO.1 Engine was turned OFF as per the QRH. We discussed briefly how this failure would impact our flight to ZZZ1 and we decided to continue as planned. Approximately 2-3 minutes later, after getting a clearance to fly direct to ZZZ (VOR), another Master Warning illuminated, Check Fire Detect and the NO.1 Engine Fuel/Fire Handle was illuminated. I [advised ATC] that we had a No. 1 engine fire and would like to return to ZZZ airport. ZZZ gave us a descent to 10,000' and a turn back towards ZZZ. We shut the number 1 engine down and secured it as per our SOP and QRH. The pilot flying (PF) in the left seat, took over the ATC communications and flew the aircraft, while I completed the remainder of the QRH check-list.We advised ATC that there were two crew onboard, our remaining fuel and that there was no hazardous cargo.We completed the QRH Descent and Approach check-lists and discussed the landing Flap setting (15) and Vref for landing. We flew a visual approach for Runway XX at ZZZ and landed at XA:22. Crash Fire Rescue vehicles followed us down the runway until we stopped. The fire crew examined the aircraft to ensure there was no fire, smoke, or leaking fluids. We were told nothing appeared abnormal, so we released the Crash Fire Rescue trucks and taxied to the apron where we shutdown the aircraft.The crew opened up the left engine nacelle to check for damage and after a short time discovered that a borescope inspection cover for the high pressure compressor case was lying on the bottom of the nacelle. This missing cover allowed extremely hot gases to exit the engine case and blow onto the Bleed Temperature sensor and the Engine Fire Loop, triggering the Hot Bleed and Engine Fire Warnings. No evidence of an actual fire was discovered. No other obvious damage was discovered at this time.
ASRSN:2164481.s: Two crew members on a Dash 8-400 ferry flight experienced false No.1 bleed hot and fire warnings shortly after departure due to a missing borescope cover allowing hot gases to trigger sensors. The crew returned to the departure airport, landed safely, and confirmed no actual fire or damage occurred.

ASRSN:2164482.n: I flew my drone without requesting LAANC authorization. I am visiting the area and was very excited to find spots to fly for recreational purposes as the natural beauty of the area is so appealing. While I had checked air space maps and apps before venturing out to the area, I thought that I was just outside the range of controlled airspace and therefore was not required to request LAANC approval. It has also been some time since I have flown and was not in the habit of making sure to obtain the necessary approvals and even though any request would have likely been auto approved I probably mistook that to mean it was not required to request. Again, I thought I was just outside the area needing approval. The drone remote did not give me any issue taking off so I thought I was in the clear. After planning for other flight locations and checking the maps I realized that I probably was required to request approval for this flight. As soon as I realized I may have flown without approval I went to the internet to see what steps I should take as I value being able to fly my drone recreationally and generally am very aware of the safety requirements and adherence to regulations to ensure proper compliance with regulations. In the future I will check multiple apps and sources of controlled airspace maps to ensure I am requesting LAANC when required and be sure to make the request as required for each flight I do.
ASRSN:2164482.s: A recreational drone pilot flew without requesting LAANC authorization, mistakenly believing the location was outside controlled airspace. The pilot realized the error post-flight after reviewing maps and plans to verify airspace requirements and obtain necessary approvals for future operations.

ASRSN:2164486.n: Aircraft X was an IFR flight that I had already cleared to land for RWY XX. I also had an Aircraft Y in the pattern to RWY XY who was cleared #2 for a touch and go. When Aircraft X was very short final, he declared he was going around due to a vehicle on the runway. At that time, I was looking up at the Aircraft Y to make sure the sequence worked and to ensure separation for a second, eastbound Aircraft Y. I had never spoken to a vehicle to allow them access to any runways, so I rescanned and still didn't see the vehicle. I stood up, stepped to the side and that was when I saw a pickup truck on RWY XX. I told Aircraft X, Roger, go around. I asked on frequency, Who is on the runway, but no one answered. I said again, There's an Ops vehicle on the runway. Who is on the runway? Ops X answered saying it was Truck Y, and he thinks something blew out of his truck. I informed him that doesn't mean the vehicle can enter the runway. I never was able to get in contact with the offending vehicle, but I did observe him exiting RWY XX at Taxiway 1. The vehicle was no factor for my touch and go on RWY XY. I confirmed with Ops X that the vehicle would not be reentering the runway. Aircraft X was instructed to enter right traffic for RWY XX and landed without incident.As this was happening, another controller called Airport Operations via the Ops line and was informed it was a contractor in the vehicle and they would be sending someone out to take care of it. There are large structural poles impeding the line of site to multiple parts of both runways. Unfortunately, the only solution would be a new Tower with fewer line of sight obstructions.
ASRSN:2164486.s: An IFR flight executing a landing on RWY XX declared a go-around due to a contractor's pickup truck on the runway, which the controller initially missed due to structural obstructions. The vehicle exited at Taxiway 1, and the aircraft landed safely after entering right traffic.

ASRSN:2164488.n: I was instructing OJT on radar west combined with all radar sectors and coordinators. My CPC-IT trainee accepted a handoff from ZZZ Approach on Aircraft X. Aircraft X was at 4000MSL landing ZZZ. ZZZ Approach called to advise they were requesting the visual approach at ZZZ and I asked them to keep Aircraft X at 4000MSL. I believed Aircraft X was in a 3800 MVA and wanted to ensure they did not descend below that altitude, which ZZZ sometimes has them assigned. ZZZ did not hear what I said so my trainee called back and reiterated, to which ZZZ replied they were level at 4000. Shortly after Aircraft X checked in on our frequency I realized they were actually farther north than I thought and were inside of a 4200 MVA. I immediately instructed my trainee to climb them to 4200 to recover the separation. A few miles later Aircraft X reported the field in sight and cancelled IFR.I believe the main factor was my trainee's different radar scope settings than my own, making it more difficult for me to discern the MVA boundaries from airspace boundaries. OJTIs (On the Job Training Instructor) should always use extra vigilance when viewing their trainee's scopes that will have different setups than their own.
ASRSN:2164488.s: An OJT instructor and trainee managed Aircraft X during a visual approach at ZZZ. The instructor misjudged the aircraft's position due to differing radar scope settings, causing a temporary loss of separation from a 4200 MVA, which was corrected by instructing a climb to 4200 before the pilot cancelled IFR.

ASRSN:2164518.n: ACARS was very intermittent at Gate XX. We had a couple maintenance writeups, aircraft was having issues initializing. Once we received all documents via the printer I released parking brake and got a warning about pushing with a notification form warning. We were never given a Dangerous Goods (DG) preliminary printout. I called Operations and they had no idea what was going on / no feedback and had to call them again. I had to ask Ramp if we had DG and the Ramp Supervisor confirmed we did have DG. They said Load Planning would be sending the Final DG Summary. We received it after about 7 minutes and pushed.
ASRSN:2164518.s: The flight crew experienced intermittent ACARS and initialization issues at Gate XX, delaying pushback due to a missing Dangerous Goods preliminary printout. After contacting Operations and confirming DG with the Ramp Supervisor, the crew received the final summary seven minutes later and pushed back.

ASRSN:2164532.n: We were given another departure on clearance when loaded in the box we realized LNAV wouldn't engage. This was a heading departure but first fix didn't load. During initial climb on ZZZZZ SID instead of continuing straight we executed a turn early and engaged lnav at 400 ft which put us directly to ZZZZZ. Departure said we turned early and wanted us to expedite through 14 for terrain. We were climbing fine and had no issues with terrain clearance. We did not receive any terrain warnings.
ASRSN:2164532.s: The flight crew experienced an LNAV engagement failure during the ZZZZZ SID departure, causing an early turn at 400 feet. Departure control instructed an expedited climb through 14,000 feet for terrain clearance, though the crew reported no terrain warnings or clearance issues.

ASRSN:2164599.n: We had a flight scheduled from ZZZ to ZZZ1 with a fuel stop in ZZZ2. I flew the first leg and we landed runway XX in ZZZ2. On the ground in ZZZ2 we noticed that the winds have shifted and now favored runway XY. It's also important to note that runway XY is the preferred take off runway. The captain and I had briefed to do the ZZZ2 ODP (Obstacle Departure Procedure). Upon getting fuel and closing the door, we finished our checklists followed our procedures and started the engines. We briefed the taxi to runway XY and I made a radio call saying that we were taxing from the FBO to runway XY. We had to cross runway XZ/XA so we looked left and right and I made the appropriate radio cal to let the CTAF know we were crossing the runway. Once clear of the runway I made another radio call. Shortly after crossing we were number 2 behind a large jet that was waiting to get their clearance to also depart runway XY. Once behind the large jet I called center on Comm 1 however I still listened to CTAF on comm 2 the captain was also listening to both frequencies. Center told me we were waiting for a airplane to land opposite direction with a tailwind" runway XX so we couldn't depart runway XY. Once that aircraft landed the large jet took the runway and departed. Center told me to expect a 3 minute delay before I would receive my IFR release. 3 minutes later we get the release they tell us to climb to 10,000 feet and they also gave us a squawk code. The captain and I briefed the changes for the departure looked left and right and prior to crossing the hold short makings I made a radio call saying we were going to be a climbing left turn then a right turn up to 10,000 feet. We heard no other radio call prior to our transmission or after our transmission that there was any other airplane near the ZZZ2 airport. We confirmed XY was the correct runway looked left and right and I spun the MFD (Multi-Function Flight Display) to display a 10 mile radius to show us any traffic or hazards. We saw nothing and took off. The captain called power set I called 70 and accelerating towards V1 the captain said is that an airplane. Before we could make it out it was too late we were past V1 had to continue. The captain lifted the airplane very slowly into the air keeping it within feet of the ground as the other airplane passed dangerously close. I asked if that other airplane was on frequency he said he was. I then made our last radio call and we made it to ZZZ1 safely." We were scheduled to fly passengers from ZZZ - ZZZ1 via a fuel stop in ZZZ2. Upon arrival in ZZZ2 we requested a quick turn, took fuel, programmed the aircraft, briefed and dual verified our departure and obstacle departure procedure for the leg to ZZZ1. I was pilot flying and the FO was pilot monitoring for this leg.Winds at the time of departure were reported at 320 @ 5kts. Runways XX & XY are listed as the preferred runways for departure. In addition, runways XZ & XA are listed as the preferred runways for arrivals. After engine start and the completion of our checklists, we made our appropriate radio call and proceeded to taxi behind a large jet flight to runway XX while monitoring both Unicom and center frequencies. We proceeded to cross runway XA/XB and again made our appropriate radio call to announce our crossing. We reached runway XX number two in sequence behind the large jet who was communicating with arriving VFR traffic 13 miles out on the ILS to XZ for a full stop. We called center and received a hold for release clearance and were advised of the large jet and the incoming VFR traffic. After the traffic arrived and called clear of the runway, the large jet inquired and received their release for departure. Center advised us to expect an approximate 3 minute delay prior to receiving our release. We held short of runway XX and monitored both frequencies. I noted that there were birds circling the end of the runway and took note to monitor them on departure. After a short time center released us for departure. We proceeded to make our radio call, taking the active runway XX for departure, verified the area was clear to the left and right, and taxied into position. It is worth noting that we could not see the departure end of runway XZ from the departure end of XX as the runway appears to crest. We verified runway XX was correct, and the FO dialed out the MFD (Multi-Function Flight Display) scale. There was no traffic indicating on the TCAS system, and neither of us heard any traffic calls for ZZZ2 airport. Power was set and we began our takeoff roll. The 70" call was made. As we were passing V1, I stated, "Is that a [expletive] airplane!" There was a mirage effect on the runway, and I was not 100% sure if what I saw was an aircraft or the birds I noted prior to departure. I quickly determined this was in fact an aircraft, but was not sure if the aircraft was arriving or departing runway XZ. I opted to hold the aircraft on and near the ground until I determined what scenario we were in. We quickly figured out the oncoming aircraft was either in a missed approach or takeoff configuration, and I opted to pass under the opposite direction traffic. We accelerated through approximately 160 kts indicated, passed under the aircraft and continued our takeoff after crossing paths. We continued on the obstacle departure for ZZZ2. Upon takeoff, the FO queried the departing aircraft. They responded jet traffic departing ZZZ2 did you hear our radio calls, we responded in the negative, and they asked if we made any radio calls to which we responded yes, plenty of them. We then left the frequency to contact Center. No erratic maneuvers were initiated, no limitations were exceeded and the passengers were never aware or made aware of any incident. We continued the flight and landed in ZZZ1 without further incident.As I replay this scenario in my head, there are only a couple suggestions and factors that we had control of that I can think of. First, the selection of ZZZ2 as a fuel stop location. In our operations small uncontrolled fields are a necessary known. However that does not mean we need to unnecessarily increase activity to those locations. From a risk analysis perspective, avoiding these fields when able lowers our potential interactions with this type of increased risk operations. Whereas the small slower airfield has benefits from a straight line stopover point, and a quick turn perspective, in the future I will look at a larger tower controlled field for fuel stops. Secondly, there are a couple knowns. The Unicom Frequency is a heavily congested frequency, and it is important to not tie up these frequencies with nonessential calls. And, I understand the AIM recommends to not ask any traffic in the area to respond for that reason. What I do not know, is if we did transmit into the blind with this request, maybe more radio calls could have changed the outcome? I will continue to follow the recommendation of the AIM as I am sure it is a calculated cost vs reward equation. And I do not know the answer here, but I do feel something needs to change in this area. I cannot 100% guarantee transmissions were not made by this other aircraft, but I can 100% guarantee that we were monitoring and did not hear them, In addition, I would hope that the pilot in the other aircraft did not hear ours... On an afternoon we are all familiar with the increased traffic of GA aircraft, is it possible that these transmission were blocked by the continuous transmissions from the skydiving operation, or the other area airports operations? I feel that something can be done better to maintain safe and efficient communications.Besides this, I feel that the holes in the Swiss cheese just all lined that day. Fortunately, we had factors that worked in our favor and tragedy was avoided."
ASRSN:2164599.s: Two pilots experienced a near mid-air collision during takeoff from uncontrolled airport ZZZ2 while departing runway XX. The incident occurred because the crew did not hear radio calls from an opposing aircraft on runway XZ, likely due to frequency congestion, forcing a low-altitude pass under the other plane.

ASRSN:2164634.n: At 2800 ft msl prior to MUDHO ON Ducks5 SID went right to right with black drone within 12-15 ft on climb out after receiving report from ATC of quadcopter drone reported by preceding aircraft. Cause: Drone activity. On RNAV departure off runway 18C climbing thru 2800 ft, black quad-copter flew within 12-15 feet of FO's (right) side of aircraft. ATC had just warned us of a previous flight departing off runway 18C having seen a drone just above them.Cause: Drone.Suggestion: No drones within airport traffic area.
ASRSN:2164634.s: During an RNAV departure from runway 18C, a black quadcopter flew within 12-15 feet of the aircraft at 2,800 ft MSL after ATC warned of a preceding drone sighting. The pilot attributed the near-miss to drone activity in the airport traffic area.

ASRSN:2164686.n: We had some smoke smell in the flight deck. None that we could see in the cabin though and shortly after we had the smoke smell we got a CAS (Crew Alerting System) message that said ALT1, ALT2, ESSBUS, MAIN BUS 1, MAIN BUS 2 failure. When we landed I could still smell it. And A/C comp popped from the circuit breaker
ASRSN:2164686.s: The flight crew reported a smoke smell in the flight deck followed by multiple electrical system failures, including ALT1, ALT2, and main bus alerts. Upon landing, the odor persisted, and the air conditioning compressor circuit breaker was found to have popped.

ASRSN:2164740.n: I was conducting a cross country trip from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. This was on the final leg of the multi leg trip. I normally alternate between the left and right tanks every 30 minutes, however on this leg I followed the Piper manual's guidance for maximizing endurance, which instructed the pilot to run one tank dry, then switch the fuel selector to the other tank. This would ensure that all of the usable fuel in one tank was consumed and result in the maximum range. Additionally it would allow me to more exactly determine my precise fuel burn that day and determine if I needed to stop short of my destination at my predetermined bingo fuel point or if I could continue to my destination and land with my minimums of 1 hour fuel remaining.Around 2.6 hours into the flight, as expected the engine coughed and I went to select the other tank. However the fuel selector would not budge and the fuel selector handle was ice cold. I reached with both hands to attempt to turn the fuel selector but was unsuccessful, a few seconds later the engine was silent and the EGTs dropped. I immediately turned towards the nearest airport, calculated that I had enough altitude to glide to the airport and informed ATC of the issue. I remembered that during my preflight I had water in one of my fuel tanks when I sumped, and it had taken multiple attempts to obtain a fuel sample without water. I suspected that there was still a small amount of water in that tank, and it had settled to the bottom near the fuel selector and frozen, causing the stuck fuel selector. I informed atc what I believed the issue was and that I would continue to troubleshoot while gliding to the airport.Knowing the likely cause of the stoppage and understanding that the solution would be to turn the stuck selector, and believing that it was caused by ice and the cold temperatures at altitude I continued my glide towards the airport while I rubbed the fuel selector with my hand in an attempt to warm it up. Around 6,000 feet I was able to begin to turn the fuel selector and was able to select the tank with fuel remaining. In a few seconds the engine roared back to life. Satisfied that the issue was fixed, and I had a full tank that was now feeding the engine I changed my diversion airport to the second nearest airport that had services as the initial airport I selected did not have any services and continued the flight uneventfully. Upon landing I consulted with an Inspection Authority (IA), and we both agreed with my assessment of water freezing in the fuel selector and the ice melting as I descended and the air warmed.
ASRSN:2164740.s: The pilot of a Piper aircraft experienced an engine failure during cruise when a fuel selector froze due to water contamination, preventing a tank switch. The pilot glided to 6,000 feet, warmed the handle by hand to restore fuel flow, and landed safely after confirming the ice melted during descent.

ASRSN:2164770.n: On the departure ATC cleared us to climb to 10000 feet, we were vectored to avoid a very powerful cell that was in the path of the departure when we were close to level 10000 we were assigned to climb via, the SID witch has a top altitude of 12000, before reaching ZZZZZ intersection we were hit by moderate to severe turbulence with altitude gains of 2000ft and loss of 1000ft. At that point the automatic pilot struggled to keep the published altitude and we got really busy handling the situation, we managed to return to 10000ft but the publish altitude was busted. ATC notified us about a possible deviation and a phone number was given
ASRSN:2164770.s: During departure, the crew encountered moderate to severe turbulence while climbing via a SID to 12,000 feet, causing altitude deviations of ±2,000 feet and autopilot struggles. The crew manually returned to 10,000 feet but busted the published altitude, prompting ATC to notify them of a possible deviation and provide a contact number.

ASRSN:2164773.n: My student and I were practicing traffic patterns for landings. After our sixth touch and go, we were making a climbing left turn from crosswind to downwind to reach pattern altitude, which is 1,100 feet. At around 900 feet, the engine sputtered, and we experienced a significant loss of RPM, dropping to about 1,500. I attempted to increase the throttle and quickly performed the emergency memory items, but I couldn't regain engine power. The propeller was still spinning, but we were down to around 700 or 800 feet, positioned between midfield and abeam the Runway XX numbers. At that point, I decided to land on Runway XX, assuming we wouldn't be able to return to Runway XY or XZ, even though Runway XY was being used for the pattern. I turned directly toward the Runway XX numbers while contacting the tower controller. Due to my panic and fast talking, the controller initially had difficulty identifying who I was. Eventually, the controller understood my situation and intentions and rerouted two aircraft on final for Runway XY while I executed an emergency landing on Runway XX. I managed to get the plane down safely, and there were no other traffic conflicts.
ASRSN:2164773.s: A pilot and student experienced a significant engine power loss at 900 feet during a climbing left turn in a traffic pattern. The pilot executed an emergency landing on Runway XX after the tower controller rerouted traffic, resulting in a safe landing with no conflicts.

ASRSN:2164801.n: Gate XX received initial dangerous goods (DG) via ACARS after 20 minutes of ACARS issues which other aircraft experienced. At approximately XA:29 received the first FINAL DG" report. Inputted the required dangerous goods acknowledgement code into ACARS, and printed out the msg for proof. At approximately XA:43 received a second "FINAL DG" via ACARS, and the report was incomplete. This DG had 3 dry ice entries in the summary section, but only 2 dry ice entries in the expanded explanation section. Attempted to figure it out with ramp via headset standard blue tooth headset issues ensued. Finally heard from ramp that they had held not boarded a section guessed maybe that was the issue but it still should have come up on the report. Tried Operations not much help, eventually the ramp reopened the weight manifest as the FINAL WEIGHT MANIFEST had come out during all of this buffoonery. Searched through FOM for guidance. Found that an item left off should indicate OFF this was not the case. Noticed that an option for pilot request of final DG notification could be obtained another way. Tried that received a report with 3 items in the header portion and 3 items in the expanded section. Entered FINAL dangerous goods acknowledgement code, received ACARS response and THEN did the before push checklist and departed normally, albeit 9 minutes late. Enroute at cruise we debriefed the departure and question arose as to whether it was the FINAL WEIGHT MANIFEST that drove the issue. Went to ACARS LOAD PLAN menu and selected FINAL WEIGHT MANIFEST. A copy of the final printed out automatically as expected, but we also received a copy of the INCORRECT FINAL DG that was sent at XA:43 along with the FINAL WEIGHT MANIFEST. We loaded the PERF INIT to get rid of the execute light after ERASE. This is the second time in the last month out of ZZZ where this Captain has received a second "FINAL" DG notification AFTER submitted dangerous goods acknowledgement code. It is a set up for getting a Captain violated for improper procedures with reference to DG. This Captain treats DG like the Maintenance Release, and pushes back on the hurry hurry hurry mode that exists at the company as we pass the 5 MIN prior to push time.Not sure how to fix this problem the weight and balance as well as DG loading is extremely opaque and after many years still does not make sense at times."
ASRSN:2164801.s: The Captain experienced ACARS issues at Gate XX where a second, incomplete "FINAL DG" report arrived after the initial acknowledgement was sent. This discrepancy caused a 9-minute departure delay and raised concerns about potential procedural violations due to opaque weight and balance systems.

ASRSN:2164806.n: During preflight we received normal preliminary Dangerous Goods (DG) paperwork. Prior to push we received a Final DG Summary and sent an ACARS message. During taxi we started receiving additional DG paperwork from the printer, including both preliminary and final. We stopped to verify it wasn't additional and it appeared to be a copy of what was previously received. To be safe I sent another DG acknowledgement message but we had already pushed. During climbout we continued to receive additional DG paperwork via the printer. There was approximately 20 pages of information and it was out of order so it was difficult to tell if it was new copies of the original information inadvertently sent again. DG paperwork normally works very smoothly and is clear and concise so this was an unusual event.
ASRSN:2164806.s: The flight crew received duplicate and disordered Dangerous Goods paperwork via the printer during taxi and climbout. This unusual event caused confusion regarding whether new information was being transmitted, though the crew verified the documents were likely copies of previously received data.

ASRSN:2164850.n: Upon receiving SVC INFO SUMMARY via ACARS, I noticed there was a lithium ion wheelchair listed. I consulted the FOM to verify that a report was not required. There was no Dangerous Goods (DG) listed upon ACARS initialization. I did however, after being airborne realize that we never received a mobility device tag from customer service.
ASRSN:2164850.s: The pilot noted a lithium-ion wheelchair on the ACARS SVC INFO SUMMARY but found no Dangerous Goods listed at initialization. After becoming airborne, the crew realized they never received a mobility device tag from customer service.

ASRSN:2164925.n: Climbing out of FL 300 flight experienced uncommanded discharge of Halon Fire Extinguisher on Flight Deck due to faulty/ failed o-ring. Loud pop" followed by loud "hissing" initially believed to be cracked/failed L2 windshield. Resulted in flight crew exposure to halon gas. Crew donned O2, secured faulty (discharged) fire extinguisher, conferred with Dispatch and medical and continued to destination without further incident. Cause: As flight crew we are trained to employ Fire Extinguishers to fight a fire. And while we are taught to utilize a protective breathing equipment (PBE) in coordination with fire fighting activities, an inadvertent discharge of a halon extinguisher has no real reference in our QRH. Consideration should be given to adding a procedure for the above eventuality."
ASRSN:2164925.s: During climb from FL 300, a faulty o-ring caused an uncommanded Halon discharge on the flight deck, exposing the crew to gas. The crew donned oxygen, secured the extinguisher, and continued to the destination, noting a lack of QRH procedures for this event.

ASRSN:2164971.n: We were on approach on the RNAV 13L into JFK. While we were in the turn I noticed two lights of phasing red and green off our right. I was PM and my FO was PF, since my FO was focused with the more critical task flying the aircraft did not have time to search for them. Based on the lights I presumed them to be drones, and their location would position them very well to film aerial footage of planes landing into JFK that night, or the filming skylights of NYC that night. They had some sort of lateral movement but not a significant amount, and difficult to judge since we were in a turn. Around 1000 feet they seemed to be below our altitude but at 500 feet seemed to be roughly at similar altitude, based on that I would estimate they were between 500-1000 ft. They were located about half a mile to a mile west northwest from runway 13R threshold. They were well out of our way and we had no risk of conflict with our approach so we elected to continue to approach and focus on our primary duties.
ASRSN:2164971.s: The Pilot Monitoring on an RNAV 13L approach to JFK observed two phasing red and green lights, presumed to be drones, located 500–1,000 feet AGL and 0.5–1 mile west-northwest of the 13R threshold. The crew determined there was no conflict risk and continued the approach to focus on primary duties.

ASRSN:2165055.n: While doing the AFD noted right traffic pattern for runway 35 at LUD, a helicopter announced intentions, entered the airspace and landed midfield on the parallel taxiway. I had been making position reports while in the pattern. I announced 'Decatur traffic XX on final, touch and go 35, Decatur'. As I approached the numbers, the helicopter announced 'lifting off'. They picked up and started north just as I started to climb out. They were above and in front of me and to my left over the taxiway. I leveled off at 1500' MSL (500' AGL) and announced on CTAF I was behind and below the helicopter. They did not acknowledge and continued straight ahead. I started to turn right to increase the horizontal distance when they announced they were turning right crosswind. We were both at about the same airspeed. I stayed at 1500' MSL (below them) and turned north to go straight out. They crossed over me and continued in the pattern.
ASRSN:2165055.s: A pilot on final for runway 35 at LUD encountered a helicopter lifting off from a parallel taxiway. The helicopter crossed above and in front of the aircraft, prompting the pilot to descend to 1500' MSL and turn right to maintain separation while the helicopter continued its pattern.

ASRSN:2165058.n: During tailwheel transition instructional flight, I was the instructor in the back seat and the pilot receiving instruction was in the front seat. Pilot made a normal 3-point (touchdown on mains and tailwheel simultaneously. The plane touched down then rose back into the air, yawing to the right about 30 degrees. Both of us applied full power for a go-around. It was a warm day and we had been flying with the left window open. I had been flying with a loose fitting cap under my headset. When full power was applied, the wind blast came in through the window and knocked my cap back, taking the headset and my glasses with it. This startled and distracted me enough that I failed to straighten the airplane out to align with the runway center line. As the airplane started to accelerate, it touched down, unfortunately headed off the runway. When I noticed this, I chopped the power to idle and pulled the stick hard back to keep the tail on the ground. As we went into the dirt, the airplane started decelerating rapidly and I then added power and steered us back on the runway. I then returned control over to the student while I fished out my gear from the floor of the airplane. Luckily, there was no damage to the airplane and no runway lights were struck. This was entirely my fault for not straitening out the airplane. I'd like to think I'm experienced enough that I wouldn't have been startled but apparently not. This event was terribly embarrassing and just proves that no one is immune in an event like this.
ASRSN:2165058.s: During a tailwheel transition instructional flight, the instructor's headset and glasses were blown off by wind from an open window during a go-around, causing distraction. This led to a runway excursion into the dirt, but the instructor recovered the aircraft with no damage.

ASRSN:2165066.n: We had a near miss at Long Beach Airport (LGB) on departure from 26R.We departed 26R and were approved for a right downwind departure. We were not given any altitude restriction. Our aircraft was Aircraft X. Aircraft Y was given instructions to cross midfield at or above 2000 feet to enter right traffic for 26R. As we were turning crosswind to downwind at approximately 1600 feet the Tower gave us a traffic alert and northbound heading to fly to avoid the traffic. We were not told to stop our climb nor were we given an altitude restriction, so we continued our climb as there was airspace up ahead at 2,500 feet that we were trying to avoid. As we continued climbing, we immediately turned to our given heading. Once on our heading we noticed a much faster Aircraft Y flying directly overhead of us with only about 100 feet of vertical distance and no more than 50 feet of horizontal distance. The aircraft had deviated from their instructions from Tower and their flight radar track showed they had prematurely started their descent to pattern altitude while simultaneously drifted over the departure end of the runway and continued straight towards us in the downwind. The controller immediately told us to stop our climb and told the other aircraft to arrest their descent. We took evasive action by pushing the nose down and starting a rapid descent as soon as we saw the other aircraft. I believe three things contributed to this event. One was the controllers lack of awareness to how fast the other aircraft was flying and also that Aircraft Y had drifted towards the departure end of the runway instead of crossing over midfield as they were instructed to do. Second was Aircraft Y drifting off course and not correcting or noticing and beginning their descent prematurely without being instructor by the Tower Controller. The final factor was myself and my student being distracted and focusing on clearing the upcoming Delta airspace that we were rapidly approaching.
ASRSN:2165066.s: Pilots of Aircraft X departing LGB Runway 26R experienced a near miss with Aircraft Y, which descended prematurely and drifted toward the departure end instead of crossing midfield at 2,000 feet. The incident resulted in only 100 feet vertical and 50 feet horizontal separation, attributed to controller oversight, Aircraft Y's deviation, and the departing crew's distraction.

ASRSN:2165070.n: Flood starting my aircraft engine on the ramp about 90 degrees to the runway . Engine started with full power, I could not reduce the power . With brakes on - accelerated toward the taxiway and runway . Crossed the taxiway, the infield, and onto the runway . I was able to kill the engine with the mixture control and roll off the runway at an intersection. This even happened very fast . I was first concerned with stopping, unable to do so I concerned myself with steering away from taxiway and runway lights. On the runway;I killed the engine with mixture and was able to roll off the runway.My mechanic and I will be checking for any binding or sticking on all engine controls to prevent this from ever happening again.
ASRSN:2165070.s: The pilot experienced an engine flood during start on the ramp, causing the engine to run at full power with no ability to reduce thrust. The aircraft accelerated across the taxiway and runway before the pilot killed the engine with the mixture control and exited at an intersection.

ASRSN:2165094.n: Two incidents happened within a short time of each other.A near miss with a helicopter. After departing ZZZ from runway XX, We first saw the helicopter with ADBS traffic alert and began looking outside for it. When we saw it, it was directly in front of us about 200-300 above us and about 1000 feet laterally. We passed beneath it realizing it was close.We proceeded to ZZZ1 for traffic pattern work. We joined the left downwind for runway XX and did two landings to a full stop. We noticed that the wind had changed to favor runway XY so we switched to XY on the ground and did two landings before departing to the south. During this whole time we were broadcasting our intentions but realized that we were on the wrong frequency and changed to the correct one around the time we switched runways.We noticed there was other traffic using XY while we were first using XX. However we continued to use XX because the AWOS clearly showed XX to the best runway for wind at that time. Later in the day we found that our radio silence had rattled nerves and caused problems for the flight school. We spoke to the flight school manger and offered our apologies for causing a disruption. There were no close calls or issues other then no communication that we observed.
ASRSN:2165094.s: The pilot reported a near miss with a helicopter 200–300 feet above after departing runway XX and later caused disruption by broadcasting on the wrong frequency during traffic pattern work. The pilot attributed the communication issue to using the incorrect frequency while following AWOS wind data, resulting in radio silence that alarmed the flight school.

ASRSN:2165100.n: I noticed that the FAA on hand had the wrong dates and looked on FAADroneZone for an updated waiver. I found two that had the adjacent site that was flying at later in the week (Original and updated one). I didn't see that the current site I was working did not have clearance for me to fly. After pulling the updated authorization, I contacted ZZZ tower to alert of operations. The operator at the tower took my information (Name/number/authorization #/etc) and then cleared me to fly. Thinking I was good to fly, I continued normal operation of UAS with no issues. On a different day, I called the tower again to let them know that we were operating again at the same site, this time we were told that we didn't have an authorization in place. All operations were cancelled.This event occurred due to not confirming/checking that we had an authorization in place for this site and confusion about another site close by. The tower personnel who is responsible for checking the information also did not accurately check our authorization number after giving all our information to them (Or they could have thought we were flying at the other site). I acknowledge that it is not towers responsibility to verify my authorization. This was breakdown in communication and confirming details before flying this operation. In the future, I will check the authorization information and all the details 2 weeks before conducting operation that requires an authorization.
ASRSN:2165100.s: A UAS operator attempted to fly at a site without valid authorization due to confusion with an adjacent location and failed verification by tower personnel. Operations were cancelled on the second attempt after the tower confirmed the lack of clearance, highlighting a breakdown in communication and pre-flight checks.

ASRSN:2165101.n: Filed LAANC via Air Control [App], received automatic authorization in the app but the text didn't come through until after the flight had landed. In the future I will wait for the text and add additional time to my flight block rather than assuming the App was the only confirmation.
ASRSN:2165101.s: A drone pilot filed a LAANC request via the Air Control app and received automatic authorization, but the confirmation text arrived only after landing. The pilot attributed the delay to relying solely on the app and plans to wait for the text and add buffer time in the future.

ASRSN:2165102.n: My flight mission was for an insurance property inspection set for Day 3. On Day 0, I submitted a flight plan through the AutoPylot app for Day 3. I had intended to set the mission time for 11am EST, but accidentally set it for 11pm-12am. I received a message I should fly with caution and that I did not need to obtain a LAANC approval. I later discovered that ZZZ airspace is uncontrolled after 11pm and before 6am but controlled between 6am-11pm. This is where my mistake occurred. In the future, when checking the AutoPylot app, I will be sure to double check my mission date and time to make sure it is an accurate representation of when I plan to fly. I will also be sure to check FAA Visualizeit website to review airspace prior to my flight missions.
ASRSN:2165102.s: The pilot submitted a flight plan via the AutoPylot app for an insurance inspection, accidentally scheduling the mission for 11pm instead of 11am. This error caused the flight to occur in uncontrolled ZZZ airspace rather than the intended controlled airspace, prompting the pilot to commit to verifying mission times and airspace status in the future.

ASRSN:2165106.n: Aircraft X was on a vector at 3000 ft. for a straight-in visual approach to Runway 16L at AFW. Aircraft Z was an unidentified target passing through the final at 2800 ft. indicated, while another VFR I didn't even get the call sign for passed through final at 2400 ft., meanwhile Aircraft Y was overhead at 4000 being vectored to DTO. Aircraft X had nowhere to go to avoid traffic, and was pulled off final to avoid the traffic, then climbed to 3500 for safety while in conflict with the 4000-ft. Aircraft Y above him. AFW needs protected airspace for their final, either a Class D extension that extends out to 10 miles from 2000 to 3000 ft., or lower the overlying Class B to 2000 to protect these planes. This same scenario happens multiple times daily and is extremely unsafe.
ASRSN:2165106.s: Aircraft X on a 3000 ft vector for Runway 16L at AFW was pulled off final due to conflicting VFR traffic at 2400–2800 ft and Aircraft Y at 4000 ft. The pilot climbed to 3500 ft for safety, citing a recurring lack of protected airspace as the cause of this unsafe situation.

ASRSN:2165110.n: The previous sector controller coordinated non-radar Aircraft X coming over the fix ZZZZZ and then established on the airway VXXX at an altitude of 120 (twelve thousand feet MSL) which according to my overhead sector charts stated was the top altitude for the route. I approved this altitude and routing into my airspace. A few minutes later Aircraft X popped up on radar and I saw that they appeared to not be established on the airway but presently at a safe altitude for their current position. Aircraft X was then advised to turn left(can't remember specific heading I gave) to join the airway and continue to maintain 12;000ft as there was a 12,600 MIA (Minimum IFR Altitude) at their immediate 12 O'clock and about 10 miles. Aircraft X made the appropriate turn in a timely manner and reported established on the airway. The data tag began to MSAW alert. I investigated the MSAW alert and verified that Aircraft X was established on the airway. I then rechecked the overhead chart to verify that 12;000ft MSL was a safe altitude for the aircraft. My supervisor then came and inquired about the airway and the safety of the aircraft reference the MSAW alert. I advised my supervisor that the aircraft was safe at the airway altitude of 12;000ft MSL. After further inspection from my supervisor it was determined that the overhead chart above the position I was working was not current at the new MEA on the victor route VXXX is 13;000ft. By the time that information was confirmed the aircraft was north and clear of the 12,600 MIA polygon and no longer required an altitude of 13;000ft MSL. Suggestion: Current overhead charts, current information.
ASRSN:2165110.s: An air traffic controller cleared Aircraft X to 12,000 feet on airway VXXX based on an outdated overhead chart, triggering an MSAW alert. A supervisor later confirmed the Minimum Enroute Altitude was actually 13,000 feet, but the aircraft had already safely passed the terrain obstruction.

ASRSN:2165116.n: During the event, I was working as a radar controller for West and East combined, responsible for all arrivals and departures. Aircraft X was handed off from Center IFR climbing to 070 MSL. Once I received communication with Aircraft X, I descended Aircraft X to 050 MSL and asked them what approach they wanted. Aircraft X eventually decided to accept the GNAV RWY 20L approach since they were parking on Location A of the airport. During the time it took for them to fly inbound from, I had Aircraft Y inbound 10 NM from the west get the field in sight at 042. I informed Aircraft X of this and offered to descend them if they would like to go for the visual approach to RWY 20L. Aircraft X decided they would accept a visual approach, take lower, and even cancel IFR once they got closer. Aircraft X started descending on their own out of 030 MSL in the 029 MSL MVA 1.5NM from the 023 MSL MVA. I did not catch Aircraft X's altitude until 10 seconds later because my attention was on other aircraft at the time. Once I realized Aircraft X was descending, I issued them a low altitude alert. Aircraft X responded they were VFR. I responded asking Aircraft X if they would like to cancel IFR. Aircraft X confirmed IFR cancellation. I relayed to Aircraft X IFR cancellation received, gave them a pattern entry, and transferred them to FAI Tower. I believe this event occurred due to the pilot's expectation they would go VFR once they got clear of clouds.Suggestion: I recommend controllers keep up their scans of IFR aircraft's altitude, especially those who are not 'regulars' at your airport. I think pilots should follow instructions for altitude restrictions and request cancellation of IFR before they alter from their altitude restriction.
ASRSN:2165116.s: A radar controller and Aircraft X were involved during the arrival phase when the pilot descended below 3,000 MSL without clearance while expecting to go VFR. The controller issued a low altitude alert after a delay, leading to the pilot confirming IFR cancellation and transferring to the tower.

ASRSN:2165178.n: We were on the arrival, course only, in LNAV, getting stepped down by ATC for an anticipated TIP TOE VISUAL for XXL. We were given traffic information about a preceding aircraft (corporate I believe). We were queried if we had the traffic in sight. I did not but I believe the captain did. I indicated that I did in fact have the field in sight and the captain reported that and we were cleared for the visual XXL and to maintain 180k until 5 DME. With the autopilot off, I began to configure from flaps 5 to gear down while descending on a visual path to XXL. At about 1500 AGL with the runway and PAPI in sight, showing 2 red 2 white, we received a call from the tower about a low altitude alert. Puzzled from this as my sight picture with XXL showed a normal visual approach path, along with verification of the 2 red 2 white PAPI indication, we briefly discussed with each other why that alert was presented to us. We then acknowledged the alert with the tower, selected our final landing configuration and landed uneventfully.
ASRSN:2165178.s: The crew conducted a visual approach to runway XXL in LNAV, receiving a low altitude alert from the tower at 1500 AGL despite a normal PAPI indication. They acknowledged the alert, completed configuration, and landed uneventfully without identifying a specific cause for the discrepancy.

ASRSN:2165182.n: Prior to this event we had two maintenance occurrences, the first maintenance event took place 10min prior to push back, our IFE (In Flight Entertainment) was not working. After the issue was successfully resolved and few minutes past departure time, we called for push back and engine start, unfortunately London airport was doing a Runway change and we waited for another 35 min or so until we pushed back. Once we disconnected from tow bar and finished starting engines, we saw a STATUS MSG ' NOSE A/G DISAGREE' , making this our second maintenance episode. We called Dispatch and Maintenance Control via satcom and were able to resolve the problem, then coordinated with Ground Control to taxi for few feet and verify that our STATUS MSG will not repeat. After all this procedures were completed we waited for another 15min or so before we could get the Maintenance Release and finally complete our respective checklist. Finally we called Ground for taxi, and we were told to continue to Runway 27R, then Tower instructed us to line up and wait behind the departing Aircraft Y. Aircraft Y was taxing in front of us (Right to left at medium fast speed) and entered the Runway, we followed it and executed Tower instructions however Tower informed Aircraft Y that another aircraft will be departing from a further down intersection prior to their departure. At this point we already entered the runway and our distance was getting closer to Aircraft Y in front of us, the FO and myself mention to the Captain that we are number 3 for takeoff, but it was to late already. The distance between us and Aircraft Y was minimum, the Captain tried to slow down to keep momentum and finish the turn of our plane and be fully lined up, unfortunately is at this point when we noticed that Aircraft Y in front of us was executing a static takeoff and their engine jet blast pushed our aircraft backwards few feet. The Captain compensated this and finally were able to get the space needed to finish the turn and get ready for take off.
ASRSN:2165182.s: The flight crew experienced two maintenance delays before taxiing to Runway 27R, where they lined up behind Aircraft Y. While waiting for takeoff, Aircraft Y's static engine start generated jet blast that pushed the crew's aircraft backward, requiring the Captain to compensate to complete the turn.

ASRSN:2165265.n: The ILS XX was NOTAMed Out of Service in ZZZ so Dispatch issued a RAIM prediction prior to us leaving ZZZ1. ZZZ was VFR and the PAPI was in service for Runway XX. While still in cruise we received an FMS/POS disagree message due to GPS jamming. We asked Dispatch for a new RAIM prediction. RAIM prediction said we would be fine for the RNP XX. ATC also said we would have GPS for the approach. We temporarily received 6 satellites just prior to commencing the approach on one GPS receiver but none on the other. That was short lived and we ended up landing using the PAPI's for the visual since neither GPS receiver even had 1 satellite for landing. I am just wondering how we can have a positive RAIM prediction but still be jammed? Luckily in this case it was VFR with PAPIs and worse case, we had enough fuel to return to ZZZ1 if necessary.GPS jamming. RAIM prediction should factor in planned GPS jamming.
ASRSN:2165265.s: The crew experienced GPS jamming during cruise and approach at ZZZ, causing FMS/POS disagree messages and loss of satellite reception despite a positive RAIM prediction. They landed visually using PAPIs, noting that RAIM predictions should account for planned GPS jamming.

ASRSN:2165282.n: We were cleared to descend to 4000 ft. on the WYNDE2 Arrival. Ahead of our flight was a B787 that was cleared to 5000 ft. I queried Approach Control to bring awareness to the fact that we were approximately 10 miles behind the aircraft. However, the winds were 110 at 25 gusting to 30 at 400 ft.The winds were pushing the vortices in the direction of our flight and creating turbulence with rolls of approximately 10 - 20 degrees and pitch deviations of 2 degrees.The Approach Controller responded to my request to work out a different solution with the following response, 'There is no other plan, you are staying behind the heavy... somebody has to follow them.'My FO developed our own escape plan just in case the turbulence got worse.We were ultimately placed behind an Airbus A350 that was also at 5000 ft. and approximately five- and one-half miles ahead of us.The landing was made successfully with no injuries or damage.Advise ORD Approach that in trail heavies should NOT be placed above non-heavy aircraft.
ASRSN:2165282.s: The crew reported severe wake turbulence while trailing a B787 at 5000 ft during the WYNDE2 arrival into ORD, caused by crosswinds pushing vortices into their path. Despite the controller refusing to alter the separation, the flight landed safely after being repositioned behind an A350.

ASRSN:2165312.n: On takeoff ZZZ Runway XXL, I noted significant pull force required to rotate the aircraft. After liftoff, I noted the airspeed trend decreasing past V2+10, so slightly reduced pull force as I was re-trimming as well as encountering an area of sink. We immediately received a GPWS alert. We were VMC and airspeed and altitude still increasing so I left pitch and thrust alone. Had any indications changed for the worse, I would have gone full thrust and pitched for V2.Cause: Winds were variable at 3 knots became a 5 knot tailwind and possible windshear on takeoff. The winds on takeoff were not indicating a tailwind nor did the windsocks.Suggestion: Would love to see this scenario in the sim. I was nanoseconds for doing a windshear escape maneuver, in IMC I would have.
ASRSN:2165312.s: The pilot reported significant rotation force and decreasing airspeed on takeoff from Runway XXL, triggering a GPWS alert due to an unforecast tailwind and possible windshear. The crew maintained pitch and thrust in VMC as airspeed and altitude continued to increase, avoiding a windshear escape maneuver.

ASRSN:2165376.n: Received initial planned Dangerous Goods (DG) message. Then we received the first of what we be 3 Final" DG messages. Sent the Report to confirm. Then we got 2 more iterations. Seems that ZZZ likes to do it multiple times on the DG, to try and trip up Captains who do the initial Report and then maybe get involved in another checklist or something. (Sarcasm intended) and do not do a Report after each "final". Then Just prior to push they change the "final"."
ASRSN:2165376.s: The flight crew received multiple conflicting Dangerous Goods messages from ZZZ, including several "Final" iterations and a last-minute change just prior to pushback. The reporter attributes this to ZZZ's practice of sending repeated updates to test if Captains report each version.

ASRSN:2165428.n: During pushback, we receive the load closeout revision XX XA:23. The FO receives the closeout and begins reviewing as I focus on the pushback operation. The FO then asks if we have a NOTOC for restricted articles onboard. I replied we did not receive any notifications for restricted articles. I ask the Pushback Driver and he said he 'didn't think so.' The FO calls Operations who said there were no restricted articles loaded. About that time, the Tug Driver calls back and said he thinks the Crew Chief loaded dry ice in the aft cargo. I said I need the NOTOC paperwork or the dry ice removed before we can proceed. We sent a message to Dispatch who replied, 'Just talked to Operations and they verify there is no NOTOC on board.' The Crew Chief later confirmed he loaded 2 boxes of dry ice. I tell the FO to work with Station Operations to have the dry ice removed. We eventually agree to be towed back to the gate and the dry ice was removed. This voided our closeout and we were delayed awaiting revision XY arriving at XB:10. The threat is not notifying the flight crew of the presence of hazardous materials on board.Dry ice was loaded in the aft cargo without informing the Captain, or Dispatch, and providing a NOTOC. Only the FO, following proper procedures, reviewing the load closeout caught the error and saved us from unknowingly transporting undocumented HAZMAT. Stress the critical importance of loading HAZMAT and informing the crew.
ASRSN:2165428.s: During pushback, the First Officer identified undocumented dry ice in the aft cargo after the Crew Chief admitted loading it without a NOTOC. The aircraft was towed back to the gate for removal, causing a delay and voiding the load closeout.

ASRSN:2165544.n: During taxi in abeam arrival gate HYD Green RSVR low level ecam. Isolated G hydraulics per ECAM. Verified QRH for follow ups. Ramp Tower reported possible puddle under left main. Began turn into gate. Upon slowing, braking erratic. Stopped aircraft. Ramp Tower reported substantial smoke on #1 main. Stopped and shut down engines. Asked Ramp to monitor and report if any fire was present while requesting Crash Fire Rescue (CFR). Informed Flight Attendants (FAs) of mechanical failure, and instructed them to remain at their stations and to standby for further instructions and that an evacuation while unlikely was possible due to smoke on the exterior of aircraft. Meanwhile ground personnel connected headset and verified no fire present. Ramp personnel towed the aircraft to the gate, and remained in comms with over interphone until CFR arrival. CFR monitored during normal deplaning. Maintenance notified, logbook entry complete. Cause: Mechanical failure. While on the ramp, taxiing to the gate, we stopped the aircraft waiting on the gate area to clear and ramp agents to get into position. We received an ECAM caution 'HYD G RSVR LO LVL.' I called out the ECAM caution and preceded to complete the ECAM procedure. The Captain checked the QRH for follow ups while I contacted the Ramp Tower and advised them we had a mechanical issue and asked if they could see any fluid leaking or pooling under the aircraft. The Controller said he could see something reflective near our #1 main gear but said it could be a metal plate. I advised him we may have a hydraulic leak. The Captain and I reviewed the INOP systems again noting that the only item was GREEN HYD. I was surprised that there were no secondary failures or other inoperative systems. We decided to attempt to taxi to the gate under power (2 engine taxi) and that we would stop the airplane immediately if we encountered anything unusual with handling or braking. We turned into the gate and the Captain started applying brakes but said something wasn't right. I could feel the brakes skipping a little. I called out for him to stop the aircraft. The Captain set the parking brake and motioned for the ramp crew to tow us in. Almost immediately, the Ramp Tower advised us of heavy smoke from our #1 main gear. I acknowledged and requested that they roll the trucks. The ramp crew connected the tug and interphone and advised us of smoke and fluid on the left gear. We told them to immediately notify us if there was any fire. They pulled us the remaining 20 feet to the gate, advised us it stopped smoking, and we started to deplane. I remained at my seat communicating as necessary to the tug driver, Ramp Tower, and Airport Rescue and Firefighting (ARFF) until the emergency was over. Of note I want to emphasize that we received no additional ECAM messages, there were no secondary failures or additional inop systems shown on the ECAM. In particular NORM BRK and N/W STRG.Cause: Mechanical failure.
ASRSN:2165544.s: Pilots experienced a Green hydraulic reservoir low level ECAM and erratic braking while taxiing to the gate, followed by smoke from the left main gear. The aircraft was shut down, towed to the gate, and deplaned safely after ground personnel confirmed no fire, attributed to a mechanical failure.

ASRSN:2165570.n: When we were taking off from ZZZ the company was having paperwork issues due to upgrading computer systems. We got a Dangerous Goods (DG) form that stated we had no DG on board. When we arrived into ZZZ1 we got our DG paperwork and had some issues that got resolved but the Ramp Agent told us we brought in one can with DG in it. So we flew with DG on the airplane and did not have paperwork for that DG. Cause: The Ramp did not check the paperwork. We were alerted by ZZZ1 Ramp and Dangerous Goods (DG) that our aircraft had a can of miscellaneous HAZMAT onboard despite the paperwork stating we had no DG on board. We had the materials moved and the paperwork corrected.Cause: It appears to be a paperwork issue with the DG shop at ZZZ.
ASRSN:2165570.s: The crew departed ZZZ with a can of hazardous materials onboard despite paperwork stating no dangerous goods were present. The Ramp Agent at ZZZ1 identified the discrepancy, causing the crew to move the materials and correct the paperwork due to a documentation error at the ZZZ DG shop.

ASRSN:2165592.n: After landing in DVL Runway 13 we taxied off at A4 and took A back to Runway 13. We check final and approach path clear, made a radio call to CTAF we were entering the runway and started to roll onto runway practicing a soft-field takeoff. Out of the corner of my eye I saw a crop duster enter the middle of the runway and start to takeoff in the opposite direction on Runway 31 without making any radio calls. In an effort to quickly get off the runway I took controls from the student and tried to flip the airplane back around and exit at A5. The radius of turn was too large and we cut the corner of the grass to get off. The crop duster tail number appeared on ADS-B as Aircraft Y. The pilot apologized that he had not seen us and asked us if we were on CTAF. I said yes and we announced entering and taking off Runway 13. I had to turn around on the runway very quickly and get off as quick as I could to avoid a mid-air accident with a crop duster who took off from the middle of the field, without making radio calls, on a runway which the prevailing winds did not align with. Thankfully, this resulted in an outcome where nobody was serious injured and only a little shaken up.Cause: I think the crop duster having a lack of situational awareness and a lack of respect for other aircraft in the vicinity operating is what truly caused this event. On my end I could have scanned for traffic a bit better earlier because I would not have entered the runway knowing his intentions. Suggestions: If the crop duster and I both had better situational awareness of surroundings. Also, if crop duster followed runway with prevailing winds.
ASRSN:2165592.s: The pilot and student practicing a soft-field takeoff on Runway 13 at DVL encountered a crop duster (Aircraft Y) taking off in the opposite direction without radio calls. The pilot executed an emergency turn to exit the runway, avoiding a mid-air collision caused by the crop duster's lack of situational awareness and failure to follow prevailing wind procedures.

ASRSN:2165682.n: While stopped and waiting for the Push at [gate] XX, I noticed a potential conflict in aircraft movement. Aircraft X at XX had started the push with no wing walkers. I was very surprised at this. While stopped and observing, I noticed a aircraft on taxiway 'B' stopped and waiting to go into the alley and gate. I was alarmed by Aircraft Y on taxiway 'A' coming towards the push out of gate XX. It did not appear the wing walkers were going to stop the push process. At a certain point I start to wail on the Car horn to get the left-wing walkers' attention of the danger. Trying to direct both wing walkers' attention on the left wing with the horn and pointing towards the conflict. Eventually ramp spotted the potential and give the stop signal. It appears the tug driver did not see the signal and continued the push for a time with an eventual stop.
