I witnessed the wing tip of passing Aircraft Y miss the tail of Aircraft Z push by only a few feet. After Aircraft Y passing and another aircraft coming down taxiway 'A', this time Aircraft A. Taxiway 'B' was still occupied by the earlier aircraft. It was clear Aircraft A was going to use 'A', same as Aircraft Y. I then exited the vehicle to tell the wing walker of the next potential hazard with Aircraft A. Seeing no decision being made by the ramp crew, I started to direct the ramp crew to get Aircraft Z off of the taxiway to give clearance for Aircraft A passage on 'A'. With the tail now clear and abeam the Vehicle Service Road (VSR), it looked visually passable by Aircraft A. With this immediate threat passed, I when to the Push Tug driver to have a conversation of what I saw. I should have had help from Aircraft Y's crew by seeing and avoiding the potential collision by STOPPING. I know the crew was aware, The FO was clearly looking and alarmed.Suggestions: After reflecting on the situation, I realize there was more I could have done to prevent the potential collision. I should have exited my vehicle sooner to stop Aircraft Y from passing until Aircraft Z had safely retreated back into the gate. While I considered driving into Taxiway 'A' to physically block the Aircraft Y, this would have resulted in a movement area incursion, which--even in an effort to prevent an accident--would have created another safety concern. I believe this incident presents a valuable teachable opportunity, and I would like to see a complete debriefing and follow-up by all parties involved. A thorough review can ensure that all aspects of the situation are addressed and that we reinforce the importance of communication and safety protocols moving forward. Involving Airfield Safety in the debrief would also help provide valuable insights and oversight.
ASRSN:2165682.s: A ground vehicle operator observed Aircraft Z pushing from Gate XX without wing walkers while Aircraft Y approached on Taxiway A, resulting in a near-miss where the wingtip missed the tail by a few feet. The operator used a horn to alert ramp crew, who eventually stopped the push, though the tug driver initially failed to see the stop signal.

ASRSN:2165683.n: The Captain gave me clearance and released the brakes to start the push back. As the push was started the part of the nose gear that attaches to the toe bar broke off and the push back had to be stopped. I realized the event occurred there was a loud pop and the tow bar disconnected from the plane. The event occurred because the bolts that were on the nose gear had snapped and released the bar that holds onto the tow bar. I informed the Captain to set the bakes as the plane was still rolling back and we contacted Maintenance and Management to inform them about what had happened.
ASRSN:2165683.s: The First Officer reported that during pushback, the nose gear tow bar attachment broke due to snapped bolts, causing a loud pop and disconnection. The aircraft was stopped immediately, and Maintenance and Management were notified.

ASRSN:2165685.n: We push out Aircraft X at Gate XX and I'm the wing walker at the Captain side, after were in the center line to stop the push my co-worker tried to remove the towbar from the tractor and he couldn't remove the towbar pin. He went to the nose gear and tried to remove but still wouldn't release. He came to me while doing an (X) sign to the pilot he ask me to try if I can remove but the same thing. The pushback driver moved the pushback tractor just to loosen the tension of the towbar thats the time the towbar dropped and the aircraft rolled. when the towbar went in between tire of the nosegeartension of the towbarwe notify our Crew Chief, and the Crew Chief notify the Manager I was the push driver on Aircraft X. The push was ok but my wing walker was having a hard time to disconnect the towbar so I decided to tell the pilot to release the brake so that I can straighten it out to release the tension on the towbar. By the time I stopped the towbar dropped and the plane start rolling towards me and the towbar went under the nose gear so I told the pilot set the brake. We manage to remove the towbar by polling it out. when I saw that the towbar went under the nose gearthe towbar came loose and the plane rollover into the towbarwe notify the Crew Chief right away
ASRSN:2165685.s: During pushback of Aircraft X, the wing walker and pushback driver struggled to disconnect the towbar, causing the driver to move the tractor to release tension. The towbar subsequently dropped and became trapped under the nose gear, causing the aircraft to roll before the pilot applied brakes and the crew manually removed the equipment.

ASRSN:2165702.n: 9000ft. Traffic alert. Watching traffic on TCAS. Saw white airplane [Aircraft Y] close to what looked like what was showing on TCAS. Called, I see traffic. Traffic getting closer on TCAS. Waiting to see which direction RA is going to give us. RA climb. Autopilot off. Put flight director in the green. Almost immediately RA guidance drops. No, Clear of Contact. Looked at right side Primary Flight Display (PFD). RA guidance dropped. Looked out left window. Aircraft Y windscreens very visible, then saw airplane in a steep right bank descending. Arrival into ZZZ. Speaking with ZZZ approach. Our aircraft had recently leveled after ATC instructions to descend from 11,000' and maintain 9000'. As we approached the ZZZZZ intersection, we noticed, on our traffic display, Aircraft Y approximately 4 miles our 11 o-clock position at an altitude above ours and descending. Rapidly, the target was turning toward our flight path and descending into our altitude. The PF visually spotted the aircraft. Within seconds, our TCAS alerted a TA that very quickly progressed into a RA. The RA directed a climb and the PF immediately complied. The RA cleared when our aircraft reached 9200. I looked at the traffic on the Multi-function Flight Display (MFD) to see it was indicated as under us at an altitude of 9000. That aircraft then continued descent as it passed behind us. While the RA was initiating, ATC made a callout to what I later learned was the other aircraft, a King Air 90. ATC was instructing, 'Traffic 1 o'clock, 1 mile, stop your descent.' The other aircraft did not verbally respond. After we cleared conflict, which was to our left and rear, I asked the PF how close the aircraft came to us. The PF replied, 'I could see both of his windscreens.' I asked if we were within 200 feet and the PF replied, 'Yes.' When the RA initiated, I notified ATC that we were responding to a TCAS RA. His response was, 'Yeah, that was my fault. Traffic is behind you now, no factor.'After landing at our destination, ZZZ, I called the TRACON supervisor. I learned that the King Air was a sky diving transport and was in the process of a rapid turning descent post sky divers away. From all indications, this was a near mid air collision. Had the PF not spotted the King Air and taken immediate evasive action when the RA initiated, I believe a collision would have been likely.I believe this occurrence had multiple contributing factors. First, the sky diving aircraft dropped jumpers over the ZZZ1 airport and then turned toward the arrival corridor, approximately 3 miles away. The King Air was maneuvering in a steep spiral to lose altitude solely for the purpose of saving time while trying to beat his jumpers to the ground. In the commercial airman certification standards, such a maneuver requires clearing the area. The King Air almost definitely didn't do this. ATC never advised us of the King Air nor his purpose. ATC had made a general call of sky diving over ZZZ1 prior to our check-on. ATC never advised of our position and altitude to the King Air until the, '1 o-clock, 1 mile' call. Lastly, when I advised ATC that we were complying with the RA, his reaction was dismissive and not within guidelines, 'Behind you now, no factor.' I believe this is very inappropriate because I had only just reported the RA and had not reported clear of conflict. I believe this all could have been avoided with better communication from ATC, better decision making from the King Air, better awareness and collision avoidance practices from the King Air, and policy to keep such operations out of the published and assigned STAR.
ASRSN:2165702.s: During arrival at ZZZ, a commercial crew encountered a King Air 90 skydiving aircraft descending into their 9,000-foot path, triggering a TCAS climb RA. The pilot executed the RA to avoid a near mid-air collision, attributing the event to the King Air's unauthorized spiral descent and ATC's failure to provide timely traffic information.

ASRSN:2165767.n: IP (Instructor Pilot) was PF during event. PF was demonstrating recovery from slow flight/stalls making calls on local practice area freq. and Aircraft Y was not heard on radio. After making clearing turns and appropriate pre-maneuver tasks were completed, Aircraft Y continued on trajectory toward the area which we were working in. Aircraft Y did not deviate causing PF to take controls and perform emergency descent to avoid possible collision. I could think that maybe I should have moved to a different area, but cloud coverage only allowed for that spot. I will make sure to announce my location more clearly and try to make myself more visible.
ASRSN:2165767.s: An Instructor Pilot performing stall recoveries in a practice area failed to hear Aircraft Y on the radio. The Instructor took controls and executed an emergency descent to avoid a collision because Aircraft Y did not deviate from its trajectory toward the maneuvering zone.

ASRSN:2165771.n: Prior to the incident, we had conducted two laps in the pattern with normal operation We were asked to land and taxi back due to traffic waiting to depart the airport. While waiting to depart for another lap in the pattern in sequence with other aircraft, we noticed a 'campfire' like smell that was intermittent. We opened windows and doors to identify source of smell and the smell dissipated. We did not see smoke when the instructor opened the door and stuck her head out to look at the exhaust. We concluded that the smell originated from an external source and continued the flight. We were holding short for several minutes with nominal engine operation. On the runway, full power was applied, verified engine instruments were green and takeoff power was normal and takeoff approximately 1500 feet down Runway XX. Per track log from Sentry/Foreflight, at 200ft AGL we experienced a drop in power and performance was not as expected. The airplane was climbing slowly and climb angle was shallower than normal to maintain adequate airspeed. The passenger (commercially rated) and instructor noted engine noise and vibration change. We turned crosswind early at 715ft AGL and kept the downwind within gliding distance. Midfield downwind the instructor noted excessive heat on shoes, legs, and in the cabin plastics and side pocket. Oil temperature and pressure were normal at this time, but EGT gauge was inop so no reading could be taken to understand state of exhaust gas temperature. EGT was squawked INOP as of a month ago and placarded prior to the flight. At this time, cabin plastics and air vents were hot to touch. I requested a short approach and full stop landing, and touched down on the 1000' markers and exited the runway immediately at [Taxiway] 1. Instructor pulled mixture and I pulled fuel cutoff, the passenger exited the aircraft first followed by the instructor and myself. My flight bag was in the baggage compartment to make room for our passenger, so prior to the flight I had put my handheld radio in the pilot side pocket in case it would be needed in flight. I called the Tower on my handheld after exiting the aircraft to notify that we evacuated the airplane due to a suspected engine fire. Fire department (FD) was called and noted that excessive temperatures were registered in the right hand cylinders about 15 minutes after landing. On exit a post-flight walk around, we also noticed that the exhaust stack was charred black which was not present before the flight. Airplane was towed back to the ramp after the FD called all-clear on fire risk. Due to the proximity to the ground and runway and need secure the aircraft prior to landing, and emergency was not declared on frequency with the Tower. There were no injuries and no external damage to the aircraft was visible on the post-flight inspection with the exception of the charred exhaust stack.
ASRSN:2165771.s: During a training flight, the pilot and instructor experienced a power loss and excessive cabin heat shortly after takeoff, suspecting an engine fire due to a charred exhaust stack. They executed a short-field landing and evacuated the aircraft safely with no injuries, though the EGT gauge was inoperative.

ASRSN:2165811.n: Student was landing on runway XX at ZZZ in rear cockpit. Instructor was in front cockpit. Student bounced landing on grass portion of runway resulting in a centerline deviation. Instructor took control of aircraft to recover from the bounced landing and scraped the right wingtip on the paved portion of the runway leading up to the runway XY/XZ intersection.The bounced landing and centerline deviation could have been resolved by adding power and initiating a go-around, allowing for a second attempt from a more stabilized approach.
ASRSN:2165811.s: A student pilot bounced on the grass portion of runway XX at ZZZ, causing a centerline deviation. The instructor took control to recover, scraping the right wingtip on the pavement, though the report notes a go-around could have resolved the situation.

ASRSN:2165816.n: We were cruising on a flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2, as a fuel stop along our route. What I am about to describe happened 20 minutes prior to the adverse event I am going to describe following this, while cruising we felt a slight 'thud' and smelt a faint chemical smell for approximately 2 minutes, everything seemed normal and no abnormalities were present, we chalked this up to turbulence or the two large dogs in the back possibly jumping or moving. (This will become important later)However, at 10;500ft MSL about 20 miles southwest of ZZZ I noticed the oil pressure gauge shift to near the bottom of the green arc. And about 20 seconds later it dropped below the green arc and we felt an engine roughness, not so much a decrease in power yet. We looked at our ForeFlight advisory glide rings and realized we were not within gliding distance of ZZZ (the nearest airport) so I suggested we climb the airplane as high as possible at Vy speed (we got up to 12;300ft MSL). As ZZZ slowly became within gliding distance, the oil pressure gauge continued to fall closer to 0. I suggested we [request priority handling] and worry about the paperwork later, but this didn't seem to convince him as we still had our engine and it was producing power. We got over the airport at 12;300ft MSL and that's when I stated our intentions on the CTAF that we were steep spiraling down to land on the runway. Around 11;000ft the engine started running very rough and I suggested we turn off the engine before it got too dangerous or violent and caused damage, as I knew we could easily spiral down with no engine and glide it to the runway, a commercial maneuver we have both practiced numerous times. However, the pilot I was flying with was not convinced to turn off the engine until it got very rough and smoke began coming inside the cockpit. (Later on he would state that we should have turned off the engine earlier, I believe he learned a lot from this experience).We were now around 9;500ft MSL when I pointed the smoke out to him and declared on CTAF that we had an engine fire and announced for everyone to clear the runway. We then pushed open our windows while simultaneously pushing the nose forward in an attempt to put out the fire, the other pilot had controls at this time and I was shutting off fuel to the engine. The fuel tank selector valve would not move from 'RIGHT' to 'OFF', we swapped roles and I continued to fly the airplane down in an attempt to put out the smoke even punching through a cloud to get it cooler. He wasn't able to shut off the fuel tank selector so we swapped roles again, as we had decided this was going to be his landing as he had over 100 hours in this aircraft specifically, where this was only my second flight in it. I then was able to get the selector to budge to the 'OFF' position. I then squawked XXXX and [advised ATC] on frequency.Once we reached approximately 4;000ft MSL the smoke coming inside the cockpit had calmed down and our engine stopped windmilling. The other pilot continued the approach to land and did another two spirals and slipped the aircraft on final to get us low enough to land. He came in fast with no flaps and we used up a lot of the available runway length, at least half. We pulled off on whatever taxiway shut off everything and hopped out of the airplane, we also instantly pulled the dogs from the baggage compartment. We were then met by two gentlemen from the FBO with a fire extinguisher and they put out the remaining smoke coming from the engine. On the ground, we noticed the spinner was missing and we believe that was the 'thud' we heard 20 minutes prior to this event. We are not sure if it punctured something as it flew off and caused a gradual oil leak, but this is the only guess we have about the two events being related. After removing the cowling, near the rear two cylinders of the engine it had thrown a cylinder rod right through the top of the engine, leaving oil everywhere and a massive hole on top of the engine block. We also noticed we must have popped the nose gear tire during landing via intense braking efforts. After being met by authorities, firefighters, and ambulance crew. The aircraft was then tugged to the FBO.
ASRSN:2165816.s: Two pilots flying a twin-engine aircraft with dogs experienced an engine failure at 10,500ft caused by a detached spinner and thrown connecting rod. They declared an emergency, struggled to shut off fuel, and landed safely with a popped nose tire after the engine caught fire.

ASRSN:2165828.n: Was flying a practice RNAV XX approach into ZZZ was flying this approach visually. At 10 miles out I made a radio call that I was on a 10 mile straight in for practice RNAV XX ZZZ. I did the same for 5 mile 3 mile and short final. I had reached minimums and had disconnected the autopilot. I could be wrong on the distance but I feel like I was less than a half mile from the threshold of XX and 100ish agl and a Pilatus pc12 crosses the hold short line and enters the runway. Other planes begin yelling for me to go around. I believe that's what I was hearing. I can't be sure because I became so focused and added power to go around and I side stepped to the right of XX. Other pilots began saying the pc12 never made a radio call and had just took off and was warning the traffic on the upwind that was turning crosswind. Finally the pc12 said he was left crosswind and departing and said sorry for the com. I flew the pattern and landed with out incident.
ASRSN:2165828.s: While executing a visual practice RNAV approach to ZZZ, the pilot initiated a go-around after a Pilatus PC-12 entered the runway without radio communication. The PC-12 pilot later apologized for the communication failure, and the reporting pilot subsequently landed without incident.

ASRSN:2165834.n: Engine failure while enroute to home field. Made an uneventful landing at a private airstrip that was on route of flight. Upon landing discovered missing fuel cap. Aerobatic flight with several moments of inverted flight time led to loss of fuel, hence running out of fuel before making it back to home field. Found fuel cap at home field, returned to airplane with cap and fueled and tested airplane was good, so was able to fly airplane back to home base.Fueler failed to put fuel cap on tight and I failed to physically check that cap was secure (something I normally do). We can never trust fuelers to properly secure fuel caps. PIC must always verify the cap is secure. Screw on caps must be checked by physically touching the cap and checking they are on tight!
ASRSN:2165834.s: The pilot experienced an engine failure en route due to fuel loss from an unsecured cap during aerobatic inverted flight, forcing a landing at a private airstrip. The incident resulted from the fueler failing to tighten the cap and the pilot neglecting to verify its security.

ASRSN:2165841.n: Student pilot flying the second solo flight to complete the ppl required hours in the local traffic pattern at tmb airport. Did the first two landings, in the third landing was instructed by tower to go around to give way to traffic. in the 4th traffic pattern tower gave a choice to land in XL or XXR and make it a fullstop. winds changed during the time to variable at 8. after landing, attempted to exit Runway via 1 and the plane skid to the grass. i moved the plane back to the runway to exit via [taxiway] 2 however tower instructed to not move the plane so i shut off the plane on the Runway and waited for the airport authorities. after they looked at my documents and reported to the fsdo I taxied the plane back to spot X where my flight school is and parked the aircraft.
ASRSN:2165841.s: A student pilot conducting solo PPL training at TMB Airport skidded off the runway onto grass while exiting via Taxiway 1 after landing in variable winds. The pilot returned to the runway, shut down the aircraft on instructions from Tower, and was later cleared to taxi to the flight school after FSDO review.

ASRSN:2165842.n: I was attempting to pinpoint the location of a fire flame up during a wildland fire from the edge of the Temporary Flight Restriction in effect. I flew further west than I intended and incurred into the TFR area. I returned out of the TFR and terminated the flight, landing safely.
ASRSN:2165842.s: A pilot flying a wildland fire mission inadvertently entered a Temporary Flight Restriction while attempting to locate a flame-up. The pilot exited the restricted area and terminated the flight, landing safely.

ASRSN:2165843.n: I launched my UAS and ascended to 53m to capture photos of the city skyline at sunset. The flight was a simple vertical ascent and did not involve any lateral movement from the takeoff position. I have a laptop in my vehicle that I use for flight planning and awareness information. My browser tabs are set on Aloft's web-based airspace map, FAA TFR lists and NOTAM lists.I refresh and consult all of these prior to each flight. The takeoff location for this flight was chosen because it was devoid of people or traffic and it was outside of the St. Louis Downtown Airport's Class D airspace. The Aloft map indicated 'Clear for Takeoff' at this location. After capturing photographs and videos for several minutes, I noticed in the camera view that there was a baseball game in progress at the stadium, which was 1.3 miles from my location. I immediately landed the aircraft.
ASRSN:2165843.s: A UAS operator launched a drone to 53m outside St. Louis Downtown Airport Class D airspace for photography. The pilot immediately landed the aircraft after noticing a baseball game in progress 1.3 miles away, despite the location being marked clear for takeoff.

ASRSN:2165844.n: I was tasked with flying an inspection of nacelle damage on a wind turbine that had recently caught on fire on a wind farm, about 10 days prior and was seriously damaged. 2 days prior to my flight, the wind turbine caught on fire again as a tech was trying to inspect the damage. They needed closeup imagery of the damage at the top of the turbine to determine if it was safe for techs to attempt to climb the tower again. The data was urgently needed to assure safety for employees and expedite the inspection. In my flight planning, I looked at the Air Control app at the farm's Operations and Maintenance building. We were well outside the Class D ring for ZZZ airport. I was given the approximate location of the turbine and believed it was still outside of the Class D ring and the UAS Facility grid ring, which had a 400 foot grid covering the airspace adjacent to the wind farm, extending an additional 4 miles until zero grid near the actual runway and tower facilities. Despite the LAANC grid being on the map, LAANC authorization is not available on apps. The area also has an MOA above 500 AGL, ZZZ MOA, but it is only hot on weekdays, not the day of our flight on Day 0. I went to the site, unfortunately without checking Air Control again, I flew my drone for the structure inspection in an approximately 30 minute flight. I never flew to 400 AGL, the bulk of the flight was between 250-350 AGL. I remained within 100 feet of the structure for the bulk of the flight, except on climb out and descent, when I was transiting to and from my LZ (Landing Zone), approximately 300 feet west of my structure. Those phases of flight were from 250 feet AGL, descending diagonally to the LZ on a mostly constant diagonal flight path in both directions. There were never any aircraft observed in the airspace for 10+ miles around throughout the inspection flight. Today, when I was processing my data, it looks like I clipped the UAS Facility Grid, a portion of the grid that extends to 400 feet AGL. At most, I believe I was .2 miles inside that grid, still many miles from 0' grid and the actual airport facilities. Unfortunately, I did not have a LAANC or DroneZone authorization. My flight was likely seen on AeroScope and/RemoteID equipment. In the event that anyone needs further information about my flight, I'd be happy to discuss it with the appropriate representatives as necessary. Please accept my apology for the errant flight, I sincerely hope I did not cause any safety or security concerns to anyone.
ASRSN:2165844.s: A drone pilot conducted a wind turbine inspection flight between 250 and 350 feet AGL without LAANC authorization, inadvertently entering a UAS Facility Grid. The pilot reported no observed aircraft during the operation but acknowledged the airspace violation and apologized for the safety concern.

ASRSN:2165896.n: During Takeoff, observed Number One engine EGT Solid Red. Performed immediate action items, [requested priority handling] and returned to ZZZ. Briefed Purser, Passenger PA, Notified ZZZ Ops on VHF. Uneventful Overweight landing RWY XX. Requested Fire Trucks to check gear for any evidence of overheating prior to taxi to the gate. Made electronic logbook entries for NO 1 Engine Overheat and Overweight Landing. Debriefed Maintenance, Dispatcher, Flight Ops/Chief Pilot. Aircraft change and new inflight crew. During debriefing, Maintenance mentioned the NO1 Engine was a high time engine on this airframe and the NO2 Engine had recently been replaced.
ASRSN:2165896.s: During takeoff, the crew observed a solid red EGT on Engine 1, returned to ZZZ, and performed an uneventful overweight landing. Maintenance later noted Engine 1 was high-time while Engine 2 had recently been replaced.

ASRSN:2165901.n: Cruising at FL350. Had to turn to avoid hitting a balloon as it transited and ascended through Class A airspace as well as RVSM airspace. This craft was launched right into a significant west coast departure bank and was seen and avoided by at least 4 airliners that I heard on frequency. ATC only sees this craft on radar as something" and ATC reported that the balloon has no transponder or other RVSM equipment. Seems dangerous to launch into this particular spot without warning to the aircraft using the system in class A and RVSM. If we didn't see the balloon and turn, this would likely be a near collision report, instead.Location was SW Colorado."
ASRSN:2165901.s: A pilot cruising at FL350 in southwest Colorado turned to avoid a balloon ascending through Class A and RVSM airspace without a transponder. The untracked craft, launched into a departure bank, was visually avoided by at least four airliners, preventing a likely near collision.

ASRSN:2165909.n: In the rush of the departure, we did not send the Dangerous Goods (DG) acknowledgement code report, verifying that we had received the Final DG Summary. We had, in fact, received the report - but it was over 9 pages long, with multiple other events taking place while it printed. Making it worse was the final weights being inserted right in the middle of the DG Summary, creating a perfect distraction. This was combined with a bulk cargo door MEL - requiring a last-minute Maintenance Release report which printed right before the DG Summary. Just to finish it all off, we didn't get the 'DG acknowledgement code report not sent' report until after takeoff because of the bulk cargo door MEL item. We briefed and discussed the bulk cargo door MEL multiple times and missed the fact that it would cause this last issue.
ASRSN:2165909.s: Flight crew failed to send the Dangerous Goods acknowledgement code report during departure due to distractions from a lengthy DG Summary, weight insertions, and a bulk cargo door MEL requiring a last-minute Maintenance Release. The MEL item also delayed the system alert until after takeoff, as the crew overlooked this specific consequence during their briefing.

ASRSN:2165914.n: While on the ILS XXC, landing traffic in front of us did not vacate the runway in time causing us to do a go around at roughly 100-200 feet. We were initially given alternate missed approach instructions to fly runway heading and to climb and maintain 3000. A few seconds later, while we were still making our missed approach callouts, ATC gave us additional instructions to turn to a heading of 320 and climb and maintain 4000. I misheard his instructions and thought he wanted us to make a right turn. A few seconds after we started turning right, ATC reiterated his instructions for us to turn left. We immediately initiated a turn back to the left and made an uneventful landing.
ASRSN:2165914.s: The flight crew executed a go-around at 100–200 feet on ILS XXC due to a runway incursion. The pilot misheard ATC's missed approach heading instruction, turning right instead of left, but corrected the error after clarification and landed uneventfully.

ASRSN:2165915.n: During preflight activities, a planned dangerous goods report printed. As our pushback time approached, we had not received a final dangerous goods report! We contacted the ramp, they didn't know that we had any dangerous goods. I then contacted dispatch to confirm if we had or didn't have any dangerous goods onboard. We agreed that it was unusual to get the planned dangerous goods report and not have any onboard! We spoke to ramp supervisors, load planners and controllers. None of them could confirm our situation. We then contacted the Chief Pilot to try and determine where the report gets generated. I don't think he understood what we were asking. As I didn't want to push not knowing for sure the status of the dangerous goods, the dispatcher and I requested documentation from the load planner and the ramp manager verifying that no dangerous goods were onboard! They did send these statements to me. The dispatcher and I then agreed that it would be safe to continue!After all this and a large delay to the flight, a final dangerous goods report was generated and printed as we departed!The flight was conducted without any incident!
ASRSN:2165915.s: The flight crew experienced a significant preflight delay because a final dangerous goods report was missing despite a planned printout. After obtaining written verification from the load planner and ramp manager that no dangerous goods were onboard, the flight departed safely once the report finally generated.

ASRSN:2165922.n: After we stopped the aircraft at Spot XX and completed the tow-in supplemental procedure, normal communication was established with the ground crew. Tow-in commenced according to SOP. During tow-in, a separate person with ramp group came driving in front of our aircraft and pointed to the solid line. We in the flight deck questioned this amongst ourselves. The tow-in crew began adjusting for the solid line and it became clear to us that contact was going to occur with the adjacent building had we continued to let the ground crew head towards the solid line. I communicated on headset that they appeared to be lining up with the wrong line, we needed the original line, the dashed line. The tug operator agreed and adjusted back, but not before getting stuck in an awkward position that the tug operator had to skillfully correct. Whoever came roaring out on a tug to redirect our tow-in crew was wrong. I understand that Gate XX is a recent addition to the widebody operation, but this could have led to contact with the building to the right of the safe area.
ASRSN:2165922.s: During tow-in at Spot XX, a ramp group member incorrectly directed the tug operator toward a solid line instead of the required dashed line. The flight crew intervened to prevent potential contact with an adjacent building, forcing the tug operator to skillfully correct the aircraft's position after it became stuck.

ASRSN:2165945.n: Once again airfield items are NOT being reported on NOTAMs. This has been an issue in the past and is starting again. Runway 7 PAPIs are out of service as only 2 of 4 lights work. Northeast windsock not illuminated at night.
ASRSN:2165945.s: The reporter noted that airfield items were missing from NOTAMs, specifically that Runway 7 PAPIs were out of service with only two of four lights working and the northeast windsock was unilluminated at night.

ASRSN:2165991.n: During busy XA00L bank Aircraft X sent pushback request. Controller Called Aircraft X and held their push. ' Aircraft X your... correction hold the push and expect Runway 08 I'll Call you back'. Controller did not hear any readback and saw the aircraft push. The potential for a conflict was major. The Aircraft X at [Gate] XX called for taxi within 5 minutes. The Controller caught the push and asked Aircraft X why they pushed. They had Comms issues and eventually came on frequency to warn the Controller that the ramp crew also had pushed them to the East and were blocking [Gate] XY.
ASRSN:2165991.s: During a busy bank, Aircraft X pushed back without clearance after the controller issued a hold instruction, creating a major conflict risk. The pilot attributed the error to communication issues and reported that ramp crew had also pushed the aircraft, blocking an adjacent gate.

ASRSN:2166032.n: The Captain and I conducted flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ airport. I was the PF on this leg and the Captain was the PM. We've received information from the ATC that there's weather at ZZZ with precipitation. I flew the ILS XXR approach followed the normal procedure. As we were on final and fully configured, we encountered gusty winds. The Captain asked if I needed assistance and I said yes. We had a positive flight control exchange and I was then assisting the Captain as PM. The Tower reported the wind direction of 240 with some gust factor. As we came closer to the runway, I saw the flight path was high, but the Captain quickly corrected it. As the Captain was rounding out, a sudden gust of wind pushed us offset the centerline. At that moment, I was looking at the further end of the runway to make sure we stayed within the runway. The aircraft touched down firmly and we were told to turn left on Taxiway 1, cross Runway XY and XXL to the terminal. We followed the instructions to the gate and the rampers were in the building due to lightning surrounding the airport. The Captain talked to the Flight Attendant (FA) and made sure everyone was not injured. We then waited about 15 to 20 mins to park at the gate. As I did the post flight check, I found the left outboard tire was low and the left inboard tire was flat. Additionally, there was some grass in the left wheel-well stowaway. I notified the Captain and he checked it and put the tire in the maintenance logbook. I performed a second walk around to double check and no other damage was found.Cause: weather with gusty winds and possible micro-burstSuggestions: go around and ask for a hold, divert to a suitable airport We were cleared by ZZZ Approach Control via radar vectors to the ILS Runway XXR. We could see the approach lights approximately 13 nautical miles out. As we approached closer clouds began to move in and obscured the approach lights. Winds were reported at approximately 240 degrees, 15 knots with gusts up to 27 knots. Additionally, rain was reported on the approach and at the airfield with the heaviest portion on the approach portion.FO was initially flying the approach and was following the approach lights to the runway on automation. As the conditions on the approach became gusty, I told FO I would take over the controls, at which point we transferred controls. I was able to see the approach lights and manually flew the approach with vertical and horizontal corrections.As I began my round out and flare, I experienced a sudden gust of wind from the right side combined with a downdraft, resulting in a very firm landing. The aircraft landed left of runway centerline (Runway XXR does not have centerline lights) and I began firmly correcting back to the centerline as the runway was wet. Since braking action was not reported we decided prior to commencing the approach to make a full flap landing vacating at 1 taxiway.I met FO during the walk around and noticed the left inboard tire was flat, and the left outboard tire appeared to be low. Cause: Gusty winds and possible micro-burst.Suggestions: Holding and or diversion to an alternate airport.
ASRSN:2166032.s: The First Officer and Captain flew an ILS approach to Runway XXR in gusty winds and rain, resulting in a firm, offset landing. Post-flight inspection revealed a flat left inboard tire and grass in the wheel well, attributed to gusty winds and a possible microburst.

ASRSN:2166040.n: In TEB on Aircraft X departing runway 1 we were instructed by tower to abort the takeoff due to an aircraft crossing the runway down field, we aborted at a speed below 80 kts. We exited the runway at taxiway J, we completed all required checklists and flows. We then were re-sequenced and departed uneventfully. Tower cleared us to line up and wait runway 1 and then subsequently cleared us for takeoff runway 1. As we passed 50 kts and taxiway K I simultaneously noticed an aircraft crossing runway 1 at taxiway Q and heard Tower cancel our takeoff clearance. We stopped prior to taxiway J and exited runway 1 there without incident. After reviewing, we confirmed the other aircraft was issued a clearance to cross the runway by ground and that we were cleared for takeoff by tower. In the future, and as our airspace gets busier we will need help from automated systems which prevent runway incursions due to human error.
ASRSN:2166040.s: Pilots of Aircraft X aborted takeoff on runway 1 at TEB below 80 kts after Tower cancelled clearance due to another aircraft crossing downfield. The incident resulted from conflicting clearances issued by Ground and Tower, prompting a call for automated systems to prevent future runway incursions.

ASRSN:2166044.n: Aircraft X was in maintenance for RETRIM NOSE LEFT with autopilot on for the second time when we were assigned this aircraft. Early in the morning Aircraft X was released from maintenance for us to fly that day. We preflighted the aircraft and all appeared to be in order including the rudder trim was centered as well as aileron trim. When we took off the airplane was hand flown through 5000 ft in coordinated flight as well as neutral control inputs on the yoke at 200 knots and above. At FL210 we got a RETRIM NOSE LEFT CAS message. We followed the check list re-trimmed the rudder and reengaged the autopilot and continued the trip. When we were in the vicinity of the FAF we discontinued the auto pilot to check the trim status in anticipation of re-trimming for approach speeds. We found the aircraft flew in coordinated flight at 200 KTS clean with the left rudder trim still excessively trimmed left. We landed with no incident and on taxi back we noticed the rudder trim was so far left the display the indicator was yellow. I called maintenance to AOG the aircraft for repair. Person A answered the phone and I explained what happened and he said MEL the auto pilot since the incident happened with the autopilot on. I said sure I'll MEL the autopilot and I'm going to send a separate AOG for excessive left trim. Person A said what's excessive trim? I told him when you have to apply large amounts of rudder trim to maintain coordinated flight. He said Textron (I think that was the vendor he stated) told him there is no such thing as excessive trim and you can fly the plane all the way to the stop of left trim. I said I don't feel comfortable doing that. He said I don't understand what excessive trim is. I asked Person A if we can patch in a call with the Person C since I was uncomfortable with the dialog to this point. Person A said I don't want to talk to Person C and preceded to question me what was excessive trim and at that point wasn't accepting of me writing an AOG. I told Person A I was going to make a few calls then. Call him back. When I called Person A back he stated he was sorry for calling me several times when he found out I was tending to the clients in our plane while waiting for the recovery. He also stated he didn't mean to appear to push me into a different direction it's just hard to fix these issues. I told Person A I understand it's challenging. I felt excessive pressure to MEL the aircraft instead of AOGing the plane for a problem that I didn't understand what exactly happened to the aircraft and this was the 3rd writeup for this problem and the rudder trim has changed from takeoff to landing without the autopilot engaged. Don't push crews into an area they aren't comfortable with.
ASRSN:2166044.s: Pilots reported a recurrent RETRIM NOSE LEFT issue on Aircraft X during cruise and approach, noting excessive left rudder trim required for coordinated flight. Maintenance personnel pressured the crew to MEL the autopilot rather than AOG the aircraft, despite the trim changing without autopilot engagement.

ASRSN:2166118.n: During boarding passenger reported to us that he had inadvertently left a lithium battery item in his checked baggage and that he was concerned. We reported in turn to Captain and put a note in the company app to alert gate agent per our SOP - see: Dangerous Goods.Later on, we got a response from Manager saying we were good to go. Per Wing tips the battery was checked and is fine.Then Ramp Supervisor comes up to the flight deck to say Nobody actually checked the bag or the lithium battery device and that he would go check it himself and report in person to the Captain. So I communicate this to the lovely gate agents who r working the flight in person since they were at boarding doorMeanwhile we r having an issue with a pet that is not contained in bag- and trying to help that customer and relocate PAX (Passenger) and animal.We have asked Captain and gate agent for a manager per our SOP - since we have requested 3 times that PAX contain animal and stow it.Then Airport Supervisor comes on and says that since the PAX and animal have crossed over the threshold of the aircraft it is not her problem it is ours to resolve. Gets aggressive with finger pointing right in FA'S face, standing too close for comfort, raising her voice/yelling etc. Also gate agents are now saying they r going to take PAX (with lithium battery issue) off the flight. Captain and crew are confused. But his bag is still going with us to ZZZ? Yes. Does not make sense. So Captain says no. PAX did the right thing by reporting. And Captain says he is already dealing with Ramp Supervisor who will be reporting directly to him, regarding lithium battery in checked bag. XA53 Gate agent says we r good to close per OPS. Captain says no he is waiting for Ramp Supervisor. And cabin crew r still trying to resolve pet issue because manager has told us that we have to resolve it ourselves. And gate agent issues a [company] app statement at XA54 gate agent saying "we need cabin Supe"XA56 I have chatted again with pet in cabin pax. She is relocating pet to window seat where the carrier will fit underneath per FAR.XA56 - gate agent states on app "FA do not want to travel with pet."Which is a complete and utter fabrication when all we r doing is making sure we are not in breach of FAR 121.589. Completely disrespectful of FAR and cabin crew.Cabin Supervisor shows up. At XA59 Gate agents and Cabin Supervisor and Airport Manager/company manager slam the door saying OPS okay with door closure. Slam the 1L closed. Captain and crew in shock because Captain is awaiting face to face report from Ramp Supervisor re LITHIUM BATTERY in CHECKED BAG!!!Gate agent did not use phrase "ready to go;" to Captain. Captain has clearly stated that he is waiting for Ramp Supervisor to report in person about the lithium battery.Breach ofFAR 121.589FAR 121.310FAR 121.309FA manual states"PRIOR TO DOOR CLOSUREPrior to door closure, all criteria from phases up to and including Prior to Door Closure on the Flight Attendant Safety Checklist must be completed. When the gate agent asks if the cabin is ready, by stating the cabin is ready for door closure, the International Purser/Purser or delegate confirms all the requirements have been met. The gate agent closes the door. The boarding door may NOT be closed if conditions outlined in the Flight Attendant Safety Checklist are not met"If the Captain has clearly stated he is NOT READY to close to the Purser and the Purser has relayed to the ground staff - why was the door slammed shut?This it leaves cabin crew and Captain to decide whether to arm doors or not. Eventually Captain gives go ahead to arm doors." Pet in Cabin FAR and SOP pursuant to my report XXXXXIssues at handA) PAX (Passenger) moved pet to middle seat which has limited under seat stowage due to electronics and life vest etc.B) PAX had animal un-restrained and not contained in carrier - per FAR. PAX resisted containing pet even after being requested twice during boarding- at which time it was reported to captain and gate agents to initiate request for a manager.3) When pet was finally contained- it was observed that pet could not slide under seat per FAR. PAX was Not rude- just non-compliant. PAX was requested to move animal to window or aisle where the carrier could be slid underneath- PAX did not comply - I don't think PAX understood that it was an FAR. I believe she got the impression she was compliant enough by merely containing the animal in carrier. maybe there was a language issue - we were trying to help her out- not give her a hard time. That's the point where our ground coworker charged us with dealing with it so they could 'close the door'I went back and PAX had complied and moved the pet to beneath the window seat in compliance with FAR and SOP. I reported to Captain and ground staff - which now included cabin Supervisor, Ground Supervisor that the Pet situation was taken care of. I knew we had an outstanding issue of lithium battery in checked bag that the Captain was attending to. C) Ground staff said Captain said close door. They said Ops had dealt with the lithium battery in cargo situation They closed the door. I had no chance to ascertain with Captain that he had given the go ahead for door closure. But door was closed and I did not want to arm door till I received ok from Captain.D) I poked my head in to ascertain whether Captain had given the okay for door closure- but he had not. He was still awaiting Ramp Supervisor face to face confirmation about the lithium battery. E) So now we have a separate issue to be covered by another report re the lithium battery.F) Door was closed without Captain Ok. And no confirmation about the lithium battery.Captain gave me okay to arm door which we did. As you can see - Gate agents say quote 'FA do not want to travel with pet' completely false information and misleading/misrepresentation of the facts.Fact is I requested manager support to get the compliance of PAX with FAR 121.589
ASRSN:2166118.s: Cabin crew reported a passenger's lithium battery in checked baggage and an uncontained pet, but ground staff closed the aircraft door without the Captain's authorization while he awaited a Ramp Supervisor's confirmation on the battery. The crew eventually armed the doors after the Captain approved, following ground staff's false claims that the cabin refused to fly with the pet.

ASRSN:2166230.n: Departed ONZ runway 22. Made my call before entering runway 'Aircraft X departing 22, left traffic to the North, Grose Ile' (to pick up IFR SID thru Bravo). On roll out I heard 'Aircraft Y 3 miles South, Grosse Ile'. (No information given on inboard, heading or anything.) After takeoff at about 400 -500ft AGL we saw a Rotorcraft to our right. I immediately leveled off, but did not make an immediate turn as this would cause losing visual on the close aircraft. We were less than 100ft below and about 200 from the aircraft. After, Aircraft Y announced that he was in downwind runway 22. (he traveled West to east in what appeared to be backward 45 degree to downwind). From the sounds of the called, I believe this was a student pilot. Aircraft Y was 'B-lining' directly to the airport or backward 45 (at 500 AGL which is rotorcraft pattern altitude) without joining a traffic pattern. This put him at 500ft AGL direct over the departure end of runway 22!!! I made a radio call to him, with no response. I understand a class G airport does not legally require radio communication, nor under part 91 require a standard traffic pattern. What the pilot did was extremely dangerous. As mentioned, before I believe he was a student or low hour pilot.
ASRSN:2166230.s: A departing fixed-wing aircraft from ONZ runway 22 encountered a rotorcraft at 400–500 feet AGL while the rotorcraft pilot ignored standard traffic patterns. The departing pilot leveled off to maintain visual contact, passing within 200 feet and 100 feet below the rotorcraft, which was flying directly over the departure end.

ASRSN:2166238.n: I was flying from ZZZ1 in a Baron B55 on an IFR flight plan to ZZZ. About an hour into the flight, 30 minutes from our destination we (two passengers, three total) had a dual alternator failure. I immediately canceled IFR and ran through my checklist accordingly. Upon arrival to the airport I followed procedure and tried to drop the gear. I could tell physically that the gear was in motion and I then verified after to see if it was down and locked. To double check I ran through the checklist and verified that the gear was down and locked and the manual extension handle couldn't move anymore. Moving forward, we continued our landing procedure into the airport and upon wheels down the gear collapsed causing the plane to slide down the runway.
ASRSN:2166238.s: A pilot flying a Baron B55 with two passengers experienced a dual alternator failure en route, canceled IFR, and manually extended the landing gear. Despite verifying the gear was down and locked, the gear collapsed upon touchdown, causing the aircraft to slide down the runway.

ASRSN:2166246.n: My student and I made all appropriate calls in the pattern for Runway XX. We did hear on the radios someone was asking for a radio check on the ground. Someone acknowledged they could hear the guy in the DA20. We were on final and saw 2 planes waiting for departure for XX. As we were coming over the runway, we hear screaming going on. The guy in the DA20 has now pulled out behind us on the runway as we were passing over very low. I took over the controls from my student as it startled her and landed not realizing my mic was hot and said [expletive]. The guy in the DA20 now realizes he's on the wrong comm and is apologizing. As he's sitting on the numbers, he's troubleshooting his comms and the plane that was behind him holding short is telling him to get off the runway and screaming you entered the runway. During this ordeal there were also 2 planes on downwind too close to each other and one was telling the other they were too close. So, there was a lot going on with improper spacing, making sure they were on correct frequencies. The DA20 never looked right/left obviously before entering the runway. He was most likely on atis frequency is what I'm guessing. Once he saw us, he realized he messed up.
ASRSN:2166246.s: A DA20 entered Runway XX while a training aircraft was on final approach, causing the instructor to take control and land. The DA20 pilot likely monitored the wrong frequency, failed to look for traffic, and entered the runway without clearance, creating a conflict with the landing aircraft and other traffic.

ASRSN:2166262.n: Running out of fuel in the main tank in the traffic pattern of the destination airport. Due to the low altitude, the decision was made to execute an engine out landing on the available runway and not to troubleshoot the engine or the fuel management. The landing was successfully performed with no damage to/impact on the aircraft. It was later determined that the engine monitor reads the tank level incorrectly. It is also suspected that the fuel burn reported by the monitor is not given correctly (under investigation). The aircraft has several tanks that separately do not hold a lot of fuel. The pilot had little experience in type and in the particular aircraft flown. All variables let the pilot believe that there is enough fuel plus reserve to make an uneventful landing.In airplanes with 'complex' fuel management and limited experience of the pilot in type and plane, extra caution and reserves should be considered when it comes to the fuel management. For future flights, the pilot will switch away from the left main tank as soon as practicable and burn all other available fuel, to make sure that there are most fuel reserves available in the left main for the approach and landing. This will be particularly important for potential IMC situations, where a missed approach and reattempt landing have to be considered.
ASRSN:2166262.s: The pilot, with limited experience in the aircraft type, executed a successful engine-out landing in the traffic pattern after the fuel monitor incorrectly indicated the main tank was empty. The incident was caused by faulty fuel level and burn readings, prompting a change in fuel management strategy to prioritize reserves in the left main tank for future approaches.

ASRSN:2166271.n: Company X is a nonprofit that provides fire protection services. Authorized to provide emergency services. As public outreach - We often assist the public with animal rescues or domestic animal rescue.On Day 0 at approx XB:00 - We were operating a UAS - AGL was about 250 with strobes illuminated.We had been operating in the area since XA:15. The community was fully aware that a drone was operating in the area and our marked vehicles was directly off a state route with cones on display for Landing Zone (LZ) as well as 5 onlookers and 1 UAS pilot. We were operating under [Part] 107.NOTE: This region is part of a MOA and authorization and confirmation that MOA was cold was done via tower on recorded line.Man who arrived on scene and obviously intoxicated indicated we were flying by his property. I advised him this was legal.UAS was visually inspected for damage and none was seen to airframe or props.This report is being made here to document a gun shot at a sUAS device by a shotgun and this was confirmed to be in our direction since we could hear the pellets landing around us on metal roofs of buildings and the vehicles parked at the Facility right next store.Company X mission is to bring emergency robotic response to rural communities throughout the state - This is our 4th gunshot at drones in the past several months.There needs to be MORE education for the general public alerting them to the criminal nature of shooting at drones in addition to educating them on this emerging technology.Moreover - There has been a wealth of misinformation regarding private property and people believing that they can shoot at aircraft. There must be a media campaign to disprove this tribal misinformation.
ASRSN:2166271.s: Company X personnel operating a Part 107 UAS at 250 feet AGL were shot at with a shotgun by an intoxicated individual near their landing zone. The drone sustained no damage, but the incident highlights a recurring pattern of public misinformation regarding the legality of shooting at aircraft.

ASRSN:2166272.n: When I went to fly my DJI Mavic Air 2, it suggested updating the system. I updated the system, and it said, 'Successful Update, ready to fly.' I went to Air Aware, filed a flight request, and got authorization to fly. After pre-checking the aircraft, I lifted off and got to 380 feet, and as I proceeded to fly over an open field 200 feet away, I lost signal to the drone, and the drone continued to fly away. I had returned home set to see if the signal was lost, but I watched the drone fly behind a tree and lost sight of it. I notified the Police since I had seen the medevac helicopter and the police helicopter fly over my residence. They said they would notify the FAA, the Hospital, and the police on the ground since the aircraft was not flying. I fly with a Firehouse ARC V drone strobe, day or night, and advised the police of this. After 30 minutes, the drone did not reconnect and did not return home, so I went to the DJI program, found out its last location, and went to it. The drone was found in the front yard, about 1200 feet further than it was on the DJI Locator app location. But the battery and strobe were missing. We searched the area yesterday evening, night, and today and did not find the battery or strobe. I notified the police via a non-emergency number when I found the drone. I notified DJI of the flyaway, and then sent it in for repair today since one of the landing legs broke off. Nothing on the ground was damaged, and there were no injuries.
ASRSN:2166272.s: A pilot operating a DJI Mavic Air 2 lost signal at 380 feet, causing the drone to fly away and land 1,200 feet distant with a broken landing leg. The battery and strobe were missing, but no ground damage or injuries occurred.

ASRSN:2166296.n: Released brakes 1 minute early in accordance with SOP, Flight Manual (FM) FOM guidance. We had NO preliminary or Final Dangerous Goods (DG). Received notification form warning and did not understand why. Queried Station and were advised we had dry ice on board. CA contacted Dispatch, and requested a Final DG. Load Planning sent DG acknowledgment code message, and continued without further issues.
ASRSN:2166296.s: The flight crew received an unexpected dangerous goods warning despite having no preliminary or final DG, which was caused by dry ice on board. After querying the station and contacting Dispatch, Load Planning sent a DG acknowledgment code, allowing the flight to continue without further issues.

ASRSN:2166346.n: Operating Aircraft X maintenance ferry from ZZZ1 to ZZZ. We prepared the aircraft via the ACARS inop checklist and departed ZZZ1. Just beyond halfway through the flight, we encountered turbulent rides at Flight Level 300. At which point we requested a climb to 360. Shortly thereafter the request was approved At which point we climbed to 360. Close to 15 to 20 minutes after being at Flight Level 360 we were notified by a cabin altitude high EICAS message and Master warning chimes. At which point the Captain and I conducted our memory items for the cabin altitude high QRC checklist. The Captain delegated the checklist to me, and he assumed the role of Pilot Flying and radio operation. I Conducted the checklist items while the Captain notified ATC. After verifying on the panel that the cabin altitude was high, we began our descent from 360 down to 10,000 feet. I completed the QRC actions in full, and Once level at 10,000 feet, the Captain and I Consulted with each other, and then with Dispatch at which point, we decided to continue to ZZZ being that the aircraft was stable and safe to continue operating. The Captain maintained operation over the flight controls and the radios while I set up for the approach and briefed the Arrival into ZZZ. After my briefing was complete, I was given back operation of the flight controls and the Captain resumed Pilot Monitoring duties. We conducted a Visual approach, backed up by an ILS to Runway XXR into ZZZ, Landed the aircraft safely and taxied to the gate without the need for emergency vehicles or assistance. We then thoroughly debriefed the flight and its event together, and departed the aircraft.
ASRSN:2166346.s: Pilots operating Aircraft X on a maintenance ferry encountered turbulence at FL300 and climbed to FL360, where a cabin altitude high warning triggered a descent to 10,000 feet. After completing the checklist and confirming stability, they continued to ZZZ, landing safely without emergency assistance.

ASRSN:2166428.n: South of LAL climbing through 13,500, I spotted an object that did not show up on our TCAS system. I queried ATC as to what it may have been, ATC replied that they had a target but no information. ATC inquired what it looked like. We flew over the object at 300 kt, it appeared to be stationary. At first I thought it may have been a drone (however unlikely at that altitude) and reported that it looked shiny/metallic and about the size between a basketball and a beach ball. In hindsight, it may have been a (more likely) a balloon of some sort. ATC mentioned they would investigate to see if it may have been related to a known operation earlier that day.
ASRSN:2166428.s: A pilot climbing south of LAL through 13,500 feet observed a stationary, shiny object not detected by TCAS. The pilot described it as balloon-sized and likely a balloon, while ATC confirmed a radar target with no flight data and agreed to investigate a possible link to earlier operations.

ASRSN:2166431.n: Aircraft was in level flight at FL390 over the ZZZ VOR. EICAS MSG C HYD QTY". Center hydraulic system pressure indicated normal, but center system quantity indicated .47 and falling. QRH accomplished.Crew requested phone patch with Dispatch. Communication quality of the connection was poor at best. Crew advised Maintenance of continuing loss of fluid quantity. Quantity decreased from .47 to .30 while on the phone patch. Through broken communications, Maintenance recommendations were for a precautionary landing at ZZZ, the closest suitable airport.[Request for priority handling] with ZZZ Center. Captain took over duties of PF and initiated an ATC descent into ZZZ. Operations gave current updated weather. As part of Captain's preflight setup, the weather and NOTAMS had been downloaded to JeppView for possible enroute diversionary airports prior to departure.On descent into ZZZ, C HYD QTY stabilized at approximately .12rf. EICAS msg "C HYD SYS PRESS" illuminated intermittently. QRH accomplished with Air Demand Pump restoring system pressure.Flap and gear extension were made early in anticipation of C HYD failure. Crew decided, for safety, to utilize Flaps 20 for landing in the event of a go around in anticipation of a total C HYD system failure. Flap and gear extension were both slower than normal. Aircraft landed on Runway XX at ZZZ without incident. Aircraft was able to turn off the runway and taxi to the ramp under its own power.Upon exterior inspection, large portions of the tail were coated in hydraulic fluid.Bridging aircraft always brings a period in which numerous maintenance issues arise. The improvements may need to be on the maintenance facilities procedures and quality control." FL390 over ZZZ VOR. EICAS MSG C HYD QTY". Quantity was at .47 and falling and the pressure was indicating normal. We proceeded to accomplish the QRH. Crew got in touch with Maintenance and were advised to divert to ZZZ. Center Hydraulic quantity was at .30 communications with Maintenance ended. We Received the current weather update from Operations.We [requested priority handling] with ZZZ Center and were vectored for a descent in to ZZZ. During the decent the Center Hydraulic Quantity stabilized at .12. We accomplish another QRH for intermittent message C HYD SYS PRESS and was accomplished with Company program.We accomplished the landing checklist with Gear down and Flaps 20. Unusually delay was noticed when extending flaps and landing gear.Safe landing was accomplished we were able to taxi to parking. Suggestion: Fix the airplanes."
ASRSN:2166431.s: The flight crew diverted to ZZZ from FL390 after the center hydraulic quantity dropped to .12 and pressure fluctuated. They landed safely with Flaps 20 and slow gear extension, attributing the leak to maintenance issues on bridging aircraft.

ASRSN:2166436.n: I was pilot flying on Aircraft X ZZZ1-ZZZ. Due to the short duration of the flight, I planned for and loaded the RNAV XX approach into the FMS while at the gate in ZZZ1. In cruise, the Captain was pilot monitoring and picked up the ATIS. The ATIS stated winds were out of the NE at roughly 060 @ 12 kts gusting 24 with Runway XX in use. The Captain then stated that he recommended Runway XY for a shorter taxi due to us running behind schedule from a late departure out of ZZZ1. The Captain stated that the runway decision was up to me and I agreed to then take Runway XY for landing. The Captain then contacted Approach to advise that we had the current ATIS and to request the RNAV XY approach. On the approach, I disconnected the autopilot around 600' AGL and proceeded to hand fly. At about 100' over the threshold, I was flying using the PAPI, became high (4 white), proceeded to input nose down pitch, and reduced power to correct. At about 50', I began to slowly input right rudder and reduce the power to idle because my speed was about VREF +15. Very shortly thereafter, the Captain called for a go around. I selected max power and began to pitch up and during this moment the Captain stated that he believed the wing struck the ground. I then repeated his statement in a question and asked if the wing had hit because I didn't feel the impact. He then responded that he indeed believed the wing struck the pavement. I then continued the climb out while he contacted Tower to report the missed approach. Tower asked for the reason and the Captain stated, unstable approach." Tower then asked if we wanted to try again for the RNAV XY or Runway XX to which I told the Captain to ask for the ILS to Runway XX. Tower acknowledged the request and vectored us for the ILS XX. While turning base, the Captain told me that he wanted to take controls to which I obliged and transferred controls to him. We were then vectored to and cleared for the ILS XX. The Captain landed on Runway XX uneventfully, then taxied to the gate and deplaned. None of the cabin crew or passengers stated that they had any injuries. After passenger deplaning was complete, the Captain called Maintenance and noted the incident in the aircraft logbook.The root cause of the incident was possibly a wing stall and subsequent dip during low flight regime and go around pitch attitude. This was caused by premature power reduction on short final with gusty winds.I should have taken the approach to Runway XX as planned. Also, I should have initiated a go around earlier as soon as I became high on the approach, or waited until about 30-20' to reduce power and decrab." First officer was PF, I was PM on approach to Runway XY at ZZZ at night. FO became unstable below 50' AGL. I observed the unstable approach and called the go around, set max thrust, checked spoilers. During the go around, the airplane sank enough to strike the left wingtip. I took the controls after we reached altitude and began setting up for Runway XX, which was better suited for the wind conditions. We landed Runway XX uneventfully. Winds were 040/14G25.Cause: Gusty winds, Night time conditions, and a relatively inexperienced First Officer caused an unstable approach and lack of adequate aircraft control during a low altitude go around.Suggestion: Increase Low time First Officer hour restrictions. I trusted that my First Officer could handle the conditions when I should have recognized that they were not in a situation that was suitable to their skill level.
ASRSN:2166436.s: The First Officer flew an unstable RNAV approach to Runway XY at night in gusty winds, striking the left wingtip during a low-altitude go-around. The Captain attributed the incident to premature power reduction and the First Officer's inexperience, subsequently taking controls to land safely on Runway XX.

ASRSN:2166483.n: Unable to get into jumpseat immediately if pilots say take your Jumpseats. Unable to use your jumpseat during flight also! Very dangerous and jumpseat is not accessible to be used during the flight. FAA & OSHA needs to address the situation because passengers and flight attendants can get hurt during the various phases of flight! Are the flight attendants supposed to stand for 4-6 hours of flight without a place to sit on the jumpseat? U cannot sit in the jumpseat at all when passengers are using the restrooms and that during the whole flight please address the situation and correct! The question is how could FAA allow such an unsafe galley and jumpseat situation ? This plane is not safe for flight attendants working in the back of the aircraft. The jumpseat locations as well as the small galley space are extremely unsafe for working crew. The flight was turbulent for most of the trip. Bumpier at times more than others. The issue arises when we need to take our jumpseats and we cannot due to passengers refusing to sit down when instructed because it's 'and emergency' to go to the bathroom. We are informers, not enforcers. The double jumpseat at door 2 blocks one lavatory, and our bodies sitting on that jumpseat tend to block a good portion of the other lavatory (the one with the jumpseat attached). While attempting to be safe passengers continue to try to use the lavatories even as we advise them to sit down, causing us to not be able to sit in our jumpseats, and forcing us to stand in conditions we don't seem safe to be up in. It's a completely unacceptable design and I am unsure how this design was allowed to be introduced into a working aircraft. If this plane continues to be made, we need designated, unsellable seats, in the last row of the aircraft so flight crew has the ability to get to a safe seat quickly. Currently, the last row of the aircraft gets filled with passengers. FAA really needs to looks into this matter for the safety of every crew member that works this plane.On top of this, the limited space in the back is also dangerous to passengers. There is no space for them to stand, they get into the galley as we are attempting to pull carts out. Carts and carriers are loose (unsecured due to needing items in them) in the galley as we are getting service ready and any bit of turbulence could be dangerous for passengers. This aircraft is unsafe. The design in the back was poorly crafted. This is not ok.
ASRSN:2166483.s: Flight attendants reported being unable to occupy jumpseats during turbulence because passengers refused to leave lavatories, forcing crew to stand in an unsafe galley design. The reporter attributed this hazard to the aircraft's layout blocking lavatory access and loose service carts, urging FAA intervention for crew safety.

ASRSN:2166534.n: I was flying public benefit flights with passengers. I completed W&B and performance calculations before the flight and all checked out within limits. On the takeoff roll for the first flight I noticed a much longer ground roll than I am used to and the climb was super slow at Vx (as little as 150FPM). This put me within about 80 feet vertical of an obstacle/tower (675AGL) we were using to navigate our route visually, and much lower than I would normally be while exiting the delta airspace. I noticed we were lower than I was comfortable with so I deviated to the right and had approximately a half mile clearance from the obstacle. The rest of the flight was uneventful.On the next flight I requested a lower passenger load that would put me even more below MTOW and again within limits. I had a better ground roll, takeoff, and climb rates of approx 300-350 FPM, which I still was uncomfortable with. The rest of this flight was uneventful, but due to the high density altitude I decided to call it a day and not perform further flight. I learned that even though the performance numbers and W&B check out, you still may not get the performance you expect or need during high density altitude days. I also suspect that the organization running the flights relies on self reporting of passenger weight, and I may have had a higher load than I thought I did. In the future I will have a much lower margin below MTOW to account for this and/or use my own scale to weigh passengers.
ASRSN:2166534.s: The pilot experienced poor climb performance and low obstacle clearance during takeoff on public benefit flights due to high density altitude and suspected inaccurate passenger weight reporting. Consequently, the pilot reduced the load for the second flight but terminated operations early, noting that calculated performance limits did not match actual results.

ASRSN:2166535.n: On the MATTY4 Arrival at 5,000 ft. after crossing ROOKR. Aircraft Y was on the same arrival. I believe that the other aircraft crossed over my aircraft at 9,000 ft. and was cleared to descend to 5,000 in front of my aircraft. In my opinion Aircraft Y was 3 - 8 miles ahead when it happened. While on the arrival I experienced severe wake turbulence followed by an abrupt uncommanded bank to the right in excess of 60 degrees and a sudden pitch down of approximately 15 - 20 degrees. Autopilot had to be disengaged in order to initiate recovery from the upset condition. The aircraft required nearly 1,000 ft. to recover and stabilize. Upon recovery I contacted ATC and stated what happened followed by the typical question of was anyone injured. No one was injured during the occurrence. I had to ask the controller what altitude and heading would they like me to maintain because they offered very little guidance in the moments following the recovery. I was told to maintain 4,000 and present heading which I [was] able to.I do not believe that ATC gave me a warning of possible wake turbulence but I could be mistaken. This situation could have been avoided it the controller would have given me a descent lower than that of Aircraft Y or a vector on the arrival that would have taken me outside the path of the other aircraft. In my opinion if I had not already had my hands on the controls before I encountered the wake turbulence I believe that with the delay of reaching for the controls the aircraft would have rolled into an inverted condition and been unrecoverable at that altitude.
ASRSN:2166535.s: The pilot on the MATTY4 arrival at 5,000 ft. encountered severe wake turbulence from Aircraft Y, causing an uncommanded 60-degree bank and 20-degree pitch down requiring autopilot disengagement. The aircraft stabilized after losing 1,000 ft. with no injuries, though the pilot attributed the upset to insufficient ATC separation and lack of wake turbulence warnings.

ASRSN:2166541.n: Offending airplane Aircraft Y made improper teardrop entry into traffic pattern for Left Downwind 18. They did not extend far away enough from the runway environment before turning to accommodate for traffic already established in the pattern. This maneuver placed them in the downwind, facing the opposite direction of traffic, 200' above pattern altitude, flying directly over my aircraft (Aircraft X) that had just turned from crosswind to downwind. Upon seeing Aircraft Y fly overhead, I inquired on CTAF if they were on frequency, to which they replied they were going to slip in behind us in the downwind. No radio calls were heard from them prior to that communication. By the time they did slip in behind us, they were less than a mile off of our tail according to ADS-B data. Primary causes of this near miss are a lack of situation awareness due to poor communication practices. Contributing factors include poor ADM (Aeronautical Decision Making), primarily the improper execution of a standard pattern entry. I was on a training flight with a new private student. We planned to fly to GPH for pattern work. I did my initial call on CTAF 122.7 when we were 10 miles to the southwest. I announced we would be coming in for pattern work, intending to overfly the field at 2300' for a tear drop entry to Runway 18. I already knew another aircraft was in the pattern also practicing touch and goes. I gave more radio calls as we got closer 5 miles out 3 miles out and when we were directly over the field. Around this time the other aircraft was silent and I was not sure if they were going to extend upwind or make some other effort to space us. We flew outbound then turned around to get established in the downwind. The other aircraft still was making no radio calls until I heard them ask if we were on frequency. I told them we were. It was then I realized we had gotten close to one another. I slowed down to make sure the other aircraft and I had room. We followed behind them extended downwind and landed safely number 2. We flew several laps like this behind this other aircraft without any incident.
ASRSN:2166541.s: A training flight in Aircraft X and Aircraft Y experienced a near miss during a teardrop entry to Runway 18 at GPH. Aircraft Y entered the pattern improperly without radio calls, flying opposite traffic 200 feet above Aircraft X, caused by poor communication and decision-making.

ASRSN:2166547.n: Checked NOTAMs before leaving for SGH and Airport Runway 6/24 wasn't NOTAMed closed at this time. In route received AWOS weather and no mention of runway closure at the end of Weather readout recording. Columbus Approach never mentioned that the Airport Runway 6/24 at SGH was closed when we stated we were going to do the visual approach for Runway 6. On final approach I made a 15;10, and 5 mile position reports stating we were inbound landing, Runway six. No one at the airport Unicom acknowledged our calls or advised that Runway 6/24 was closed.Upon landing, the Captain commented about debris on the approach end of the runway and called Unicom about the debris and was told that the debris is a couple of bricks and small yellow X. We can see the wind had blown it askew. Corrective action on this situation was discussed between the crew and corrective action will be to check NOTAMs via iPad in flight after listening to the local AWOS broadcast to confirm and catch any last minute NOTAMs that come up while in route. On the Airport side, the little yellow X they use needs to be larger, more secure, and more visible to pilots on final approach. The one they used just looked like debris blown onto the runway.
ASRSN:2166547.s: The flight crew attempted a visual approach to Runway 6 at SGH, unaware the runway was closed due to missing NOTAMs and unacknowledged Unicom calls. They landed on debris mistaken for a small, wind-blown yellow X, prompting a plan to verify NOTAMs in-flight and recommending larger, more secure runway closure markers.
